topics.topic_name: Definition and Scope
topics.explanation: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, and data from unauthorized access and digital attacks. Just like you lock your house to prevent theft, cybersecurity uses digital locks and protections to keep your information safe.
topics.real_world_example: When you shop on Amazon and enter your credit card number, cybersecurity protects that information from hackers who might steal it and misuse it.
topics.why_it_matters: Without cybersecurity, your personal photos, passwords, bank accounts, and private messages could be stolen or deleted by criminals. Your entire digital life would be at risk.
topics.key_takeaway: Cybersecurity is about keeping the bad actors out and ensuring only trusted people can access your information.

topics.topic_name: The CIA Triad - Three Pillars of Security
topics.explanation: Every security system is built on three fundamental principles. Understanding CIA Triad helps you see how security protects you from different angles.

pillars.simple_definition: Only authorized people should see the data
pillars.example: Your Instagram password should only be known by you. If someone else knows it, your confidentiality is broken.
pillars.real_scenario: A company keeps employee salaries confidential. Only HR and finance teams can see it, not the entire office.

pillars.simple_definition: Data should not be changed without permission
pillars.example: When you check your exam results online, those scores should remain exactly as the teacher entered them. If someone changes 45 to 95 without permission, integrity is broken.
pillars.real_scenario: A hospital patient's medical records must not be altered by unauthorized people. Changing a blood type could harm the patient.

pillars.simple_definition: Authorized people should be able to access data when they need it
pillars.example: If Gmail is down for maintenance, you cannot access your emails. This is an availability problem.
pillars.real_scenario: During exam season, if the school's result server crashes, students cannot check their marks when needed.

topics.topic_name: Common Threats
topics.explanation: These are the most common ways attackers try to harm you. Knowing them helps you avoid falling victim.

threats.what_is_it: Software designed to damage or disable your computer or steal information from it
threats.real_example: You download what looks like a free game, but it actually contains code that records every keystroke you type. Now the attacker knows your passwords, credit card numbers, and private messages.
threats.how_it_spreads: Infected email attachments, cracked software downloads, fake antivirus programs
threats.warning_sign: Your computer runs slowly, strange pop-ups appear, or files go missing

threats.what_is_it: Fake messages or links designed to trick you into giving away passwords or personal information
threats.real_example: You receive an email saying 'Your Amazon account is locked! Verify here.' You click the link, enter your password on a fake website, and the attacker now has access to your real Amazon account and can buy things using your money.
threats.how_it_spreads: Fake emails, WhatsApp messages, SMS texts, fake websites that look identical to real ones
threats.warning_sign: Email from a 'trusted' source asking you to verify passwords or update payment information

threats.what_is_it: Malware that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them
threats.real_example: A school principal receives an email with 'Exam_Results_2024.pdf'. She opens it thinking it's legitimate. Suddenly, all files on the school's computer get encrypted and a message appears: 'Pay $5000 in Bitcoin or your files are gone forever.'
threats.how_it_spreads: Email attachments, suspicious downloads, compromised websites
threats.warning_sign: Locked files with a message demanding payment

threats.what_is_it: Using manipulation and deception to trick people into revealing confidential information
threats.real_example: You receive a call: 'Hi, this is your bank calling. We need to verify your account. Can you give us your One-Time Password (OTP)?' You trust the caller voice and share the OTP. Now the attacker can access your bank account.
threats.how_it_spreads: Phone calls pretending to be from banks, fake emails from 'support teams', impersonation on social media
threats.warning_sign: Urgent requests for passwords, OTPs, or personal information over the phone

topics.topic_name: Attack Vectors - How Attackers Gain Access
topics.explanation: An attack vector is the path or method an attacker uses to reach their target. Just like a burglar chooses between a window, door, or roof to enter a house, attackers have multiple ways to target you.

vectors.description: Sending malicious links or infected files through email
vectors.example: An email arrives saying 'You've won an iPhone!' with a link. When you click it, malware downloads to your computer.
vectors.prevention: Never click links or download attachments from unknown senders

vectors.description: Exploiting unencrypted networks or hacking into WiFi to intercept data
vectors.example: You connect to free WiFi at an airport. An attacker sitting nearby has hacked into that network and can see all passwords and credit card information you type.
vectors.prevention: Avoid using public WiFi for sensitive activities like banking

vectors.description: Gaining direct access to a computer or device to steal data or install malware
vectors.example: Someone leaves their laptop unattended in a cafe. A thief sits down, plugs in a USB drive, and copies all the files.
vectors.prevention: Never leave your devices unattended in public places

vectors.description: Using social platforms to gather information or trick people into revealing secrets
vectors.example: A fake Facebook profile claims to be your friend and asks you to share your mother's maiden name for 'verification'. This is often used as a security question for password recovery.
vectors.prevention: Be cautious about what information you share publicly online

vectors.description: Infected USB drives or devices left in public places to trick people into plugging them in
vectors.example: Someone leaves a USB drive in the parking lot labeled 'Salary Information.xlsx'. When an employee plugs it in to check what's inside, malware instantly infects the office network.
vectors.prevention: Never plug in unknown USB devices or external drives

topics.topic_name: Defense-in-Depth - Layered Security
topics.explanation: Defense-in-depth means using multiple layers of security instead of relying on just one. If one layer fails, others still protect you. Think of a castle with a moat, outer wall, inner wall, and guards - multiple obstacles to slow down attackers.
topics.analogy: A bank doesn't just have a strong front door. It has security guards, cameras, locked vaults, and alarms. Even if someone breaks through the door, other protections stop them.

security_layers.what_it_is: Locks, security cameras, guards, and restricted access
security_layers.example: Your office building has key card access - only employees can enter

security_layers.what_it_is: Firewalls and network security to block unwanted traffic
security_layers.example: Your WiFi router requires a password. Without it, strangers cannot connect

security_layers.what_it_is: Software protections like antivirus and encryption
security_layers.example: Banking apps encrypt your password so even the bank cannot see it in plain text
Your photos are backed up to cloud storage so you don't lose them if your phone breaks

security_layers.what_it_is: Teaching people to recognize threats and practice good habits
security_layers.example: Companies train employees to not click suspicious links or share passwords

topics.key_idea: No single security measure is perfect. Multiple layers ensure that if one fails, others keep protecting you.

topics.topic_name: Practical Activity - Identify Threats in a Mock Organization
topics.explanation: Let's apply what we learned. Below is a scenario of a small company. Identify the security problems and explain how each attack vector is being exploited.
topics.scenario: TechStart is a 50-person company that creates mobile apps. Here's what happens one day: An HR manager receives an email saying 'Update your employee benefits here' with a link. She clicks it and enters her password. The same morning, an employee downloads cracked software to avoid buying a license. A customer's USB drive is found in the parking lot with 'Customer Database' written on it. The company doesn't have a firewall, and employees use the same WiFi password for a month.

questions.question: What security threats does TechStart face?
questions.answer: 1. Phishing attack on HR manager - social engineering vector. 2. Malware from cracked software - dangerous download. 3. Physical attack vector - USB drive in parking lot. 4. Weak network security - no firewall and shared password.

questions.question: Which CIA Triad principle is violated in each threat?
questions.answer: 1. Phishing: Confidentiality (password exposed). 2. Cracked software: Integrity (files can be modified). 3. USB drive: Confidentiality (data exposed). 4. Weak WiFi: All three principles at risk.

questions.question: How can TechStart use defense-in-depth to prevent this?
questions.answer: Install a firewall, require strong passwords, train employees about phishing, use antivirus software, back up data, implement multi-factor authentication, secure the office entrance, and change WiFi password regularly.

topics.learning_goal: Understanding how multiple vulnerabilities can exist in one organization and how they must be addressed together.

units.title: Unit 2: Operating System Security Basics
units.description: Learn how to secure the devices people actually use - Windows, macOS, and Linux

modules.title: Operating System Security Basics
modules.description: Learn how to secure the devices people actually use - Windows, macOS, and Linux

topics.topic_name: Operating System Basics - Windows, macOS, Linux
topics.explanation: An Operating System (OS) is the software that controls your computer. Windows, macOS, and Linux are the three most common OSes. Each has its own security features you need to understand.

os_overview.who_uses_it: Most personal computers and businesses use Windows
os_overview.security_feature: Built-in Defender antivirus, Windows Defender Firewall

os_overview.who_uses_it: Apple computers, many designers and developers
Servers, developers, security experts, and tech-savvy users
os_overview.security_feature: Built-in permissions system, no single point of vulnerability
os_overview.common_on: Web servers, cloud systems, Android phones underneath

topics.topic_name: File Permissions and Access Control
topics.explanation: File permissions control who can read, write, or execute files. Think of them as rules on a file that say 'Who is allowed to do what with this file?'
topics.core_concept: Every file has an owner and permission rules. These rules prevent unauthorized people from seeing or modifying sensitive files.

permission_types.what_it_means: You can view or open the file
permission_types.example: You can read your own school notes, but not your teacher's answer key

permission_types.what_it_means: You can modify or delete the file
permission_types.example: You can edit your own document, but not someone else's project

permission_types.what_it_means: You can run the file as a program
permission_types.example: Only the operating system can execute certain system files, not regular users

topics.real_world_example: In Windows, your Documents folder has Read and Write permissions for you. Your friend's computer cannot access it because they don't have permissions. A malware trying to modify system files will fail because it doesn't have Write permission.
topics.why_it_matters: Without proper permissions, a hacker could read your private documents, modify important system files, or delete everything on your computer.

topics.topic_name: User Accounts and Access Control
topics.explanation: User accounts are identities on a computer. Each account has different permission levels. The OS uses accounts to track who did what and to enforce security rules.

account_types.what_it_can_do: Full control - install software, change settings, access all files, delete anything
account_types.real_example: Your parent's account on the family computer - they can install games, add new user accounts, change WiFi settings

account_types.what_it_can_do: Limited control - run programs, create files, but cannot install software or change system settings
account_types.real_example: Your account on the family computer - you can play games and do homework but cannot install software or change WiFi password

account_types.what_it_can_do: Minimal control - temporary access, cannot install programs or save files permanently
account_types.real_example: When a friend uses your computer, you can create a guest account for them

account_types.what_it_can_do: Special account for running background services and programs
account_types.real_example: Antivirus software runs under its own service account so it can scan all files

topics.security_principle: You should use a Standard User Account for daily work, not an Administrator account. This limits damage if your account gets hacked.

topics.topic_name: User Authentication - Passwords
topics.explanation: Authentication is proving you are who you claim to be. The most common method is a password - a secret code only you know.

what_makes_a_strong_password.why: Longer passwords take much longer to crack. A 6-character password can be cracked in seconds; a 12-character password takes days or weeks

what_makes_a_strong_password.requirement: Mix of uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols
what_makes_a_strong_password.why: Variety makes it harder to guess. 'Password123' is weak; 'P@ssw0rd!Secure2024' is strong
Attackers can guess passwords using your birthday, pet's name, or favorite sports team
If one password leaks, attackers try it on all your other accounts. Using one password for everything is dangerous
Hackers use software that tries all dictionary words first

topics.real_example: Weak password: 'MyDog2010' (uses personal info and a dictionary word). Strong password: 'Tr0pic@lSunset#92x'
topics.password_management: Use a password manager like Bitwarden or 1Password to store complex passwords. You only need to remember one master password.
topics.common_mistake: Writing passwords on sticky notes or sharing them via email or WhatsApp. Never do this.

topics.topic_name: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
topics.explanation: MFA adds a second layer of verification beyond just your password. Even if someone steals your password, they still cannot access your account without the second factor.
topics.how_it_works: You need two different things to log in: Something you know (password) + Something you have (phone) or Something you are (fingerprint)

mfa_methods.how_it_works: A code is sent to your phone via text. You enter this code after your password
mfa_methods.example: You log into Gmail, enter your password, then a text arrives: 'Your Google verification code is 123456'. You enter 123456.
mfa_methods.cons: SMS can be intercepted by advanced attackers

mfa_methods.how_it_works: An app on your phone generates a code that changes every 30 seconds. You enter this code after your password
mfa_methods.example: You use Google Authenticator app. It shows '456789' on your screen. You enter this code to log in.
mfa_methods.cons: If you lose your phone and didn't save backup codes, you're locked out

mfa_methods.how_it_works: Your fingerprint, face, or iris is scanned to verify your identity
mfa_methods.example: You unlock your iPhone using Face ID. You log into your bank, and it asks you to scan your fingerprint.
mfa_methods.pros: Very hard to fake, very convenient

mfa_methods.how_it_works: A physical device like a USB key is required to log in
mfa_methods.example: You insert a YubiKey (small USB device) into your computer, then tap it to verify login

topics.real_scenario: A hacker steals your Instagram password through phishing. They try to log in. Instagram sends a code to your phone via Authenticator app. The hacker doesn't have your phone, so they cannot get the code. Your account stays safe.
topics.recommendation: Use Authenticator apps or biometrics for important accounts (email, banking, social media)

topics.topic_name: Account Management - Principle of Least Privilege
topics.explanation: Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) means giving people only the minimum permissions they need to do their job. Nothing more, nothing less.
topics.why_it_matters: If an account gets hacked, attackers can only do what that account is allowed to do. Limited permissions = limited damage.

examples_of_PoLP.what_they_need: Access to financial files and accounting software
examples_of_PoLP.what_they_don't_need: Access to employee personal files, IT security systems, or customer data
examples_of_PoLP.wrong_approach: Give them administrator access to everything
examples_of_PoLP.right_approach: Give them access only to accounting software and financial folders

examples_of_PoLP.what_they_need: View student names and contact numbers to schedule appointments
examples_of_PoLP.what_they_don't_need: Access to grades, medical records, or teacher evaluations
examples_of_PoLP.wrong_approach: Give them access to the entire student database
examples_of_PoLP.right_approach: Give them access only to names and phone numbers

examples_of_PoLP.what_it_needs: Permission to read and copy files for backup
examples_of_PoLP.what_it_doesn't_need: Permission to delete files or modify them
examples_of_PoLP.wrong_approach: Give the service full administrator access
examples_of_PoLP.right_approach: Give it read-only permission and write access to the backup folder only

topics.role_based_access_control: Instead of giving individual permissions, you assign roles. A role is a set of permissions grouped together. Example: Cashier role can view prices and process payments but cannot change prices.

topics.topic_name: Updates and Patches - Why They Matter
topics.explanation: Software has bugs and security holes. Developers release updates and patches to fix these problems. Ignoring updates puts your device at serious risk.
topics.what_is_a_patch: A patch is a small update that fixes a specific bug or security hole without changing how the software works
topics.what_is_an_update: An update is a larger release that may add new features and fix multiple bugs

why_updates_are_critical.explanation: Hackers discover holes in software all the time. Updates close these holes before attackers can exploit them
why_updates_are_critical.example: In 2021, Microsoft released an urgent patch for Windows because hackers were exploiting a hole to take over computers. People who updated were safe; those who didn't were hacked.

why_updates_are_critical.explanation: Software bugs can cause crashes, data loss, or unexpected behavior. Patches fix these
why_updates_are_critical.example: Your bank app had a bug where it showed the wrong balance. An update fixed it.

why_updates_are_critical.explanation: Updates can make software run faster and use less memory
why_updates_are_critical.example: Your phone was running slow. You updated to the latest iOS, and now it's noticeably faster

why_updates_are_critical.explanation: Updates ensure your software works well with new devices and other software
why_updates_are_critical.example: A new printer won't work with your old Windows version. An update fixes compatibility

topics.real_world_disaster: In 2017, the WannaCry ransomware attacked 200,000 computers in 150 countries. Victims' files were encrypted and they were asked to pay in Bitcoin. Most were large organizations that hadn't updated Windows. A patch that fixed the vulnerability had been released months earlier.
topics.when_to_update: Update your device regularly - ideally immediately when prompted, or at least weekly. Don't ignore update notifications.

topics.topic_name: Firewall Basics - What It Does and How to Enable It
topics.explanation: A firewall is a security system that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic. It acts like a security guard at a door, deciding what traffic is allowed in and out.
topics.how_a_firewall_works: The firewall examines every packet of data trying to enter or leave your computer. Based on rules, it either allows or blocks the traffic.
topics.firewall_analogy: Imagine your computer is a house. A firewall is a security guard at the front door who checks everyone trying to enter. Trusted people (legitimate software) get in. Strangers (malware) get blocked.

what_a_firewall_protects_against.example: A hacker tries to connect to your computer to take control. The firewall blocks the connection attempt.
You accidentally installed malware. It tries to send your data to a hacker's server. The firewall blocks this outgoing connection.
An attacker scans your computer for open ports to find vulnerabilities. The firewall doesn't respond, making it harder to target your device.
A worm tries to spread from an infected computer to yours over the network. The firewall stops it at the network level.

types_of_firewalls.how_to_check: Settings > Privacy & Security > Windows Security > Firewall
Click the lock icon and enable firewall
Terminal command: sudo systemctl status firewalld

types_of_firewalls.enabled_by: Built into most modern routers (provides network-level protection)

topics.important_note: A firewall is not antivirus. Antivirus detects malware already on your device. A firewall prevents unauthorized access to your device. You need both.

topics.topic_name: Practical Activity - Configure Firewall, Set Up MFA, Apply Patches
topics.explanation: Now let's apply what we learned by completing three practical security tasks on your device.

activity_1.task_name: Task 1: Enable and Configure Your Firewall
activity_1.objective: Ensure your firewall is enabled and protecting your device
steps_windows: Click 'Privacy & Security' in the left sidebar
Verify that the firewall is ON for all networks (Domain, Private, Public)
If any are off, click them and toggle to ON
Close the window - your firewall is now protecting you
steps_mac: Open System Preferences (Apple menu > System Preferences)
Click the lock icon and enter your password
Click 'Firewall Options' to set rules for specific apps if desired
steps_linux: Type: sudo ufw status to verify it's active
activity_1.what_to_look_for: Green checkmark or 'ON' status next to firewall information
activity_1.success_message: Your device is now protected by a firewall

activity_2.task_name: Task 2: Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on Your Email Account
activity_2.objective: Add a second layer of security to your most important account
steps_gmail: Follow the prompts to add your phone number
Choose to receive codes via SMS or Authenticator app (app is more secure)
Google will send you a test code - enter it
Save your backup codes in a safe place (in case you lose your phone)
2FA is now enabled on your Gmail
steps_microsoft: Add a phone number for verification
Microsoft sends a code - enter it to confirm
Your account now has two-factor authentication
steps_setup_authenticator_app: Download Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator app from your phone's app store
When adding 2FA to your account, choose 'Authenticator app' instead of SMS
A QR code appears - scan it with your authenticator app
The app now generates codes for your account
This is more secure than SMS
activity_2.what_to_look_for: Confirmation message saying '2-Step Verification is on' or 'Two-Factor Authentication enabled'
activity_2.success_message: Your email account is now protected with MFA

activity_3.task_name: Task 3: Check for and Apply Operating System Updates
activity_3.objective: Ensure your device has the latest security patches
steps_windows: Windows will search for available updates
If updates are available, click 'Install now'
Your computer may restart - save your work first
After restart, verify by going back to Update & Security to confirm you're up to date
steps_mac: Click the Apple menu in the top-left
Click 'System Preferences' (or 'System Settings' on newer macOS)
If updates are available, click 'Update Now'
Your computer may restart - save your work first
After restart, verify that you're on the latest version
steps_linux: Type: sudo apt update (on Debian/Ubuntu-based systems)
Type: sudo apt upgrade to install all available updates
Wait for all updates to complete
Some updates may require a restart - type: sudo reboot
steps_check_browser: Chrome: Click the three dots menu > Help > About Google Chrome (auto-updates)
Firefox: Click the hamburger menu > Help > About Firefox (shows version and auto-updates)
Safari: Click Safari menu > About Safari (shows current version)
activity_3.what_to_look_for: Message saying 'Your device is up to date' or 'No updates available'
activity_3.success_message: Your device now has the latest security patches and is protected against known vulnerabilities

activity_completion_checklist: Firewall is enabled on your device
MFA is enabled on your email account
Operating system is updated to the latest version
Browser is updated to the latest version
topics.summary: You've now completed all three critical security tasks. Your device and email account are significantly more secure. Continue to check for updates monthly and review your security settings regularly.

units.title: Unit 3: Network Security Fundamentals
units.description: Learn how data travels across networks and how to protect it in transit

modules.title: Network Security Fundamentals
modules.description: Learn how data travels across networks and how to protect it in transit

topics.topic_name: Network Basics - TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, and Ports
topics.explanation: A network is a collection of connected computers sharing data. To understand network security, you need to know the basics of how computers communicate.

sub_topics.what_it_is: TCP/IP is the set of rules that computers use to communicate over the internet. Think of it as the language computers speak to each other.

breakdown.tcp: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) ensures data is sent reliably. It checks that all data arrives and in the correct order. Like sending a letter with confirmation of delivery.
breakdown.ip: IP (Internet Protocol) handles the addressing and routing. It's like the postal system - it ensures your message reaches the right address.

sub_topics.real_example: When you send a WhatsApp message, your phone breaks it into tiny pieces (packets). Each packet has your IP address and the recipient's IP address. The packets travel through the internet and get reassembled on the other end.
sub_topics.security_note: Without encryption, someone on your network could intercept these packets and read your messages or steal data.

sub_topics.what_it_is: DNS translates human-readable website names into IP addresses that computers understand.
sub_topics.how_it_works: You type 'google.com' in your browser. Your computer asks a DNS server 'What is the IP address for google.com?' The DNS server responds '142.251.41.14'. Your browser then connects to that IP address.
sub_topics.real_example: You visit Facebook.com. Behind the scenes, your computer queries a DNS server to find Facebook's actual IP address, then connects to it.
sub_topics.security_risk: DNS spoofing: An attacker can intercept DNS queries and give you the wrong IP address. You think you're visiting your bank, but you're actually on a fake website controlled by the attacker.
sub_topics.protection: Use secure DNS services like Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google DNS (8.8.8.8) instead of your ISP's DNS.

sub_topics.what_it_is: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network. Without DHCP, you'd have to manually type in IP addresses for every device.
sub_topics.how_it_works: When you connect to WiFi, your phone sends a request. The DHCP server (usually your router) responds with 'You are IP address 192.168.1.100'. This happens automatically.
sub_topics.real_example: You bring your laptop to a coffee shop and connect to their WiFi. DHCP gives your laptop a temporary IP address so you can browse the internet.
sub_topics.security_risk: Rogue DHCP server: An attacker sets up a fake DHCP server that hands out IP addresses and routes all your traffic through their computer. They can see everything you do.
sub_topics.protection: Connect only to trusted networks. Use VPN on public WiFi.

sub_topics.what_it_is: Ports are like doors on your computer. Different services use different ports. Port 80 is for websites (HTTP), Port 443 is for secure websites (HTTPS), Port 25 is for email.

port_examples.description: Encrypted websites with a padlock in your browser
Email servers use this to send emails
Secure Shell for remote server access
Database servers listen on this port
Uploading and downloading files (outdated, use SFTP instead)

sub_topics.real_example: When you visit www.google.com, your browser connects to port 443 on Google's server. Google's web server listens on port 443 and responds with the website.
sub_topics.security_risk: Open ports are entry points. If port 3306 (MySQL) is open to the internet, attackers can try to hack into the database.
sub_topics.protection: Close unnecessary ports. Use firewalls to block dangerous ports. Only open ports that are needed for your services.

topics.topic_name: Network Segmentation - VLANs and Isolating Critical Systems
topics.explanation: Network segmentation means dividing a network into smaller, isolated sections. If one section is breached, attackers cannot easily access other sections.
topics.why_it_matters: Imagine a hospital where doctors, patients, administrative staff, and IT equipment are all on the same network. If a patient's laptop gets infected with malware, it could spread to the entire hospital, including critical systems. With segmentation, the patient network is isolated.

segmentation_concept.without_segmentation: All devices on one big network. One breach = entire network is compromised. Like a building with no doors - a thief can steal from any room.
segmentation_concept.with_segmentation: Network divided into separate zones. Each zone has its own security rules. A breach in one zone doesn't automatically compromise others. Like a building with locked doors between sections.

vlan_explanation.what_is_vlan: VLAN stands for Virtual Local Area Network. It's a way to split one physical network into multiple logical networks using software.
vlan_explanation.simple_analogy: Your apartment building has one WiFi router, but you create three separate WiFi networks: one for living room, one for bedrooms, one for guests. Guests cannot see what's happening in your bedroom - same building, but isolated networks.
vlan_explanation.how_it_works: A switch (network device) assigns devices to different VLANs based on port numbers or MAC addresses. Devices in different VLANs cannot talk to each other without going through a firewall.

real_world_example.vlan_1: Customer service area - employees using computers to help customers. VLAN can access public data only.
real_world_example.vlan_2: Finance department - handles sensitive financial data. Encrypted and heavily protected.
real_world_example.vlan_3: IT and servers - critical systems. Very restricted access.
real_world_example.vlan_4: Guest WiFi - for visitors. Completely isolated from everything else.
real_world_example.benefit: If a visitor's infected laptop connects to guest WiFi, it cannot reach the bank's sensitive data. The malware is confined to the guest network.

network_segmentation_zones.what_goes_here: Public-facing servers like web servers, email servers, DNS servers
network_segmentation_zones.protection: Firewall controls traffic between DMZ and internal network
Only necessary ports open. Firewalls between zones.

network_segmentation_zones.what_goes_here: Network administration systems, backup servers, security monitoring
network_segmentation_zones.protection: Separate from other networks. Only admins can access.
Completely isolated. Cannot access internal systems.

topics.implementation_benefit: Even if attackers breach one segment, they're stuck there. They cannot easily move to other segments without breaking through additional firewalls and security controls.

topics.topic_name: Firewalls and Routers - Stateful vs. Stateless Filtering
topics.explanation: A firewall is a security system that filters network traffic. There are two main filtering approaches: stateless and stateful. Understanding the difference is crucial for network security.

stateless_filtering.what_it_is: Stateless firewalls examine each packet independently without remembering previous packets. Each packet is judged on its own merits.
stateless_filtering.how_it_works: A packet arrives. The firewall checks: Is the source IP allowed? Is the destination port allowed? If yes, it passes. If no, it blocks. The firewall doesn't remember this packet once it decides.
stateless_filtering.analogy: A security guard at a building entrance checks IDs one by one. He checks 'Is this ID valid?' but doesn't remember if he already let this person in today. Each entry is a fresh check.
stateless_filtering.real_example: A stateless firewall rule: 'Allow traffic from IP 192.168.1.10 to port 80'. Every packet from that IP going to port 80 is allowed, regardless of whether it's a response to an outgoing request or an unsolicited incoming packet.
stateless_filtering.drawback: Vulnerable to spoofed packets. An attacker can create a fake response packet and trick the firewall into allowing it.
stateless_filtering.when_used: Older networks or simple rules where performance is critical

stateful_filtering.what_it_is: Stateful firewalls remember the state of connections. They track which connections are active and only allow responses to legitimate outgoing connections.
stateful_filtering.how_it_works: When you make an outgoing connection, the firewall remembers it: 'Computer A is talking to Server B on port 443'. When data comes back from Server B, the firewall recognizes it as a response to the original connection and allows it.
stateful_filtering.analogy: A bouncer at a nightclub remembers who he let in. When the same person tries to leave and come back, he recognizes them. If a stranger tries to enter, he checks their ID.
stateful_filtering.real_example: Your computer makes a request to Google.com (port 443). The stateful firewall records this connection. Google responds with web data. The firewall recognizes this as a response to your request and allows it. An unsolicited packet from a hacker trying to connect to your computer is blocked because there's no matching outgoing connection.
stateful_filtering.advantage: Much more secure. Blocks most attacks without requiring detailed rule configuration.
stateful_filtering.when_used: Modern networks, most organizations, important systems

router_security.what_a_router_does: A router connects your local network to the internet. It forwards packets between networks.
router_security.router_as_firewall: Most home routers have built-in firewalls. They use stateful filtering to protect your devices.
router_security.real_example: Your home router blocks incoming connections by default. When you browse a website, the router allows the response back in because it recognizes it as a response to your request.

topics.topic_name: Intrusion Detection - IDS/IPS Concepts
topics.explanation: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors network traffic for suspicious activity. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) does the same thing but can also block attacks automatically.

ids_basic_concept.what_it_is: IDS is like a security camera that watches your network. It records suspicious activity and alerts you, but doesn't stop the attack.
ids_basic_concept.how_it_works: IDS monitors all network packets. It compares them against known attack patterns. If it detects something suspicious, it logs it and sends an alert to the security team.
ids_basic_concept.analogy: A smoke detector detects fire and sounds an alarm. It doesn't put out the fire - it just warns you. You have to take action.
ids_basic_concept.real_example: An employee's computer suddenly starts sending large amounts of data to an IP address in North Korea. The IDS detects this unusual behavior and alerts the security team. They investigate and find malware.
ids_basic_concept.response: Security team is notified, but the attack continues until they manually investigate and stop it

ips_concept.what_it_is: IPS combines detection and prevention. It monitors traffic AND automatically blocks attacks.
ips_concept.how_it_works: IPS monitors network packets. When it detects an attack, it automatically drops the malicious packets and/or blocks the connection.
ips_concept.analogy: A sprinkler system detects fire AND puts it out automatically. It both detects and prevents.
ips_concept.real_example: An attacker tries to exploit a known vulnerability in your web server. The IPS detects the attack pattern and immediately blocks the malicious packets. The attack is prevented before it succeeds.
ips_concept.response: Attack is blocked automatically without human intervention needed

detection_methods.how_it_works: IDS/IPS compares traffic against a database of known attack patterns (signatures)
detection_methods.example: SQL injection attacks follow a known pattern. The system recognizes 'SELECT * FROM users' in an HTTP request and blocks it.
detection_methods.weakness: Cannot detect new, unknown attacks (zero-day exploits)

detection_methods.how_it_works: IDS/IPS learns normal network behavior and alerts when behavior deviates significantly from normal
detection_methods.example: Normally your database sends 100 queries per minute. Suddenly it's sending 10,000 queries per minute. This is detected as an anomaly.
detection_methods.weakness: Can have false positives - normal spikes might trigger alerts

detection_methods.how_it_works: IDS/IPS uses rules and logic to detect suspicious activity
detection_methods.example: Rule: 'If someone tries to connect to 100 different ports on your server in 1 minute, it's probably a port scan attack'
detection_methods.weakness: Requires careful rule configuration to avoid false positives

real_world_scenario.situation: A bank's network is under attack
real_world_scenario.with_ids_only: IDS detects the attack and alerts the security team. The team investigates, but by then the attacker has already stolen customer data.
real_world_scenario.with_ips: IPS detects the attack and automatically blocks it. The attacker's malicious packets never reach the bank's systems. No data is stolen.

topics.important_note: IPS is more proactive than IDS, but it can sometimes block legitimate traffic if rules are too strict. IDS gives more control but requires faster human response.

topics.topic_name: VPN Basics - Encryption in Transit and Remote Access Security
topics.explanation: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secure tunnel through the internet. All your traffic is encrypted and routed through a VPN server, hiding your identity and protecting your data.

why_vpn_matters.problem: When you use public WiFi at a cafe, your internet traffic is visible to anyone on that network. An attacker can see your passwords, messages, and browsing history.
why_vpn_matters.solution: A VPN encrypts all your traffic and routes it through a secure VPN server. Even if someone intercepts your data, they cannot read it.

how_vpn_works.step1: You connect to a VPN server
how_vpn_works.step2: VPN encrypts all your internet traffic
how_vpn_works.step3: Encrypted traffic is sent through the VPN server
how_vpn_works.step4: VPN server decrypts the traffic and sends it to the destination website
how_vpn_works.step5: Website's response comes back through the VPN server
how_vpn_works.step6: VPN encrypts the response and sends it to you
how_vpn_works.result: Your ISP, network administrator, and anyone monitoring the network cannot see your traffic

vpn_analogy.without_vpn: Sending a postcard through the mail. Anyone handling it can read the message.
vpn_analogy.with_vpn: Putting the postcard inside a locked box and sending it. Only the recipient has the key to open the box and read the message.

real_world_example.scenario: You're working from a coffee shop and need to access your company's internal files
real_world_example.without_vpn: You connect directly to the cafe WiFi. The attacker intercepts your traffic, sees you logging into your company account, and steals your password.
real_world_example.with_vpn: You connect to the cafe WiFi and then connect to your company's VPN. All traffic is encrypted. The attacker only sees encrypted packets and cannot read anything.

types_of_vpn.what_it_is: Connects a single user to a corporate network securely
types_of_vpn.use_case: An employee working from home connecting to the office network

types_of_vpn.what_it_is: Connects entire networks together securely over the internet
types_of_vpn.use_case: Connecting two office locations as if they were on the same network
types_of_vpn.example: A company with offices in New York and London - they have a VPN tunnel connecting both offices

types_of_vpn.what_it_is: Hybrid - one user connects to an entire remote network
types_of_vpn.use_case: A contractor accessing a specific customer's network
types_of_vpn.example: A freelancer contractor connecting to a client's internal development network

vpn_encryption.what_is_encrypted: All data between your device and the VPN server is encrypted
vpn_encryption.what_is_not_encrypted: Data between the VPN server and the destination website is not encrypted by the VPN (it depends on the website using HTTPS)
vpn_encryption.important: Use HTTPS websites (look for the padlock) even with VPN for end-to-end encryption

vpn_for_remote_access.scenario: During COVID, many employees worked from home
vpn_for_remote_access.challenge: How do they securely access company files and systems from home?
vpn_for_remote_access.solution: Company provides VPN access. Employees connect to VPN to access internal resources as if they were in the office.
vpn_for_remote_access.security: All data is encrypted. Even if the home WiFi is hacked, the attacker cannot see company data.

vpn_limitations.limitation: VPN only encrypts data to the VPN server
vpn_limitations.clarification: Data between VPN server and destination website still needs HTTPS for full protection

vpn_limitations.limitation: VPN providers can see your traffic
vpn_limitations.clarification: Trust the VPN provider. Use reputable companies with no-log policies
Encryption and routing through an extra server takes a tiny bit of extra time. Usually not noticeable.
Netflix, banks, and some services detect and block VPN traffic to prevent account sharing

topics.best_practice: Use VPN when on public WiFi. Use it when you want privacy from your ISP. Use a reputable VPN provider with strong encryption (AES-256) and no-log policy.

topics.topic_name: Practical Activity - Network Diagram and Packet Tracing
topics.explanation: Now let's apply network security concepts by creating a network diagram and understanding how data travels through it.

activity_1.task_name: Task 1: Create a Basic Network Security Diagram
activity_1.objective: Design a network with proper security zones and understand data flow
activity_1.what_you_will_learn: How networks are segmented, where firewalls are placed, and how traffic flows between zones
activity_1.diagram_description: You will create a diagram showing: Internet, Firewall, DMZ (with web server), Internal Network (with employees and database), VPN users, and how they connect

network_components.what_it_is: Security guard between internet and internal network
Private network with employees and databases

step_by_step_instructions: Draw the Internet on the left (large cloud or circle)
Draw a Firewall as the first barrier
Draw the DMZ section with a Web Server in it (this is the public-facing part)
Draw another Firewall between DMZ and Internal Network
Draw the Internal Network with employee computers
Draw the Database Server in a separate, more protected area
Draw VPN connection from outside (remote user) through VPN gateway to the internal network
Add labels to show: traffic allowed from Internet to Web Server only, traffic from Web Server to Database requires firewall approval, Remote users can access internal network via VPN
diagram_rules: Firewall separates DMZ from Internal Network
Database server is isolated and requires multiple approvals to access
VPN users must authenticate before accessing internal network
All outgoing connections from employees can happen, but unusual outgoing connections should be monitored
what_to_label: Label all ports used (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, Database 3306, etc.)
Show firewall rules on the arrows
example_rules_to_add: Internet → Web Server: Allow port 80 and 443 only
Web Server → Database: Allow port 3306 only
Employee Computer → Internet: Allow port 443 (HTTPS), block port 25 (SMTP) to prevent email spam
VPN User → Database: Allow only if authenticated and authorized
success_criteria: Diagram shows clear separation between Internet and Internal Network
Firewalls are placed at critical boundaries
DMZ is separate from Internal Network
Database is in the most protected zone
Traffic flow arrows with rules are labeled

activity_2.task_name: Task 2: Trace a Packet's Journey Through the Network
activity_2.objective: Understand how data travels from your computer through the network to a destination
activity_2.what_you_will_learn: How packets are routed, which firewalls they pass through, and how security is applied at each step

scenario_1.title: Scenario: Browsing a Website from Inside the Office
scenario_1.person: Alice is an employee in the office

packet_journey.what_happens: Alice's browser creates an HTTPS request to google.com (port 443). The request includes: Source IP: 192.168.1.100 (Alice's computer), Destination IP: 142.251.41.14 (Google's server)
The firewall checks: Is this from an authorized internal IP? Is it going to port 443? Yes to both. The firewall ALLOWS this packet. The firewall is stateful, so it remembers this connection.

The router sees the packet is going to an IP outside the internal network (142.251.41.14). It adds the company's public IP address as the source: Source IP: 203.0.113.50 (company's public IP), Destination IP: 142.251.41.14
The packet travels across the internet through many routers. Each router looks at the destination IP and forwards it closer to Google's server.
Google receives the request and sees it's coming from IP 203.0.113.50. Google's server responds with the Google homepage encrypted (HTTPS).
Google's response packet travels back through the internet with: Source IP: 142.251.41.14 (Google), Destination IP: 203.0.113.50 (company)
The firewall recognizes this packet as a response to Alice's outgoing connection (it's stateful and remembers). It ALLOWS the packet back in.
The router sees the packet is for the company's IP. It translates the destination back to Alice's internal IP: Destination IP: 192.168.1.100 (Alice's computer)
Alice's browser receives the encrypted response, decrypts it (because it's HTTPS), and displays the Google homepage. Alice can now search Google.

security_points: The firewall allowed outgoing connection and remembered it
HTTPS encrypted the data in transit
Google never saw Alice's internal IP - only the company's public IP
Firewalls checked both outgoing and incoming packets

scenario_2.title: Scenario: Remote Employee Accessing Company Database via VPN
scenario_2.action: Bob connects to the company VPN and tries to access the customer database

packet_journey.what_happens: Bob's computer creates a connection to the VPN server with a request: 'I want to access database.company.internal'. The request is encrypted.
The encrypted VPN packet is sent to Bob's router. The router doesn't know what's inside (it's encrypted), so it just forwards it to the VPN server.
The encrypted packet travels through the internet. Even if someone intercepts it, they cannot read it because it's encrypted.
The VPN server receives Bob's encrypted request. It decrypts it and verifies: Is Bob's username and password correct? Does Bob have permission to access the database? Yes to both.
The VPN gateway creates a connection to the database server on behalf of Bob. The request goes: Source IP: 10.0.0.5 (VPN gateway), Destination IP: 10.0.0.50 (database server), Port: 3306
The firewall checks: Is this from the VPN gateway? Is it going to the database server on the correct port? Yes. The firewall ALLOWS this connection.
The database server receives the request. It retrieves the customer data and sends it back to the VPN gateway.
The VPN gateway receives the database response. It encrypts it and sends it back through the internet to Bob's home computer.
Bob's computer receives the encrypted response, decrypts it, and displays the customer data on his screen.

security_points: All traffic was encrypted by the VPN - the attacker cannot see what data Bob accessed
VPN gateway authenticated Bob before allowing access
Firewall verified the VPN gateway had permission to access the database
Database access is logged - the company knows Bob accessed it and when

scenario_3.title: Scenario: Attack Attempt - Hacker Trying to Access Company Database
scenario_3.person: Charlie (attacker) is trying to hack into the company network
scenario_3.action: Charlie tries to connect to the company's database server directly

what_happens.action: Charlie's computer sends a connection request directly to the company's database server. Source IP: 192.168.X.X (Charlie's IP), Destination IP: 203.0.113.50 (company's public IP), Port: 3306 (database port)
The firewall receives Charlie's packet. It checks the rule: 'Allow port 3306 from internet?' NO - port 3306 is for internal use only. The firewall BLOCKS this packet and logs the attempt.
The IPS detects multiple attempts to connect to port 3306 from the same external IP. It recognizes this as a port scanning attack. The IPS automatically blocks all future packets from Charlie's IP.
The security team receives an alert: 'Detected intrusion attempt on port 3306 from IP 192.168.X.X'. They investigate and find it's a brute-force attack. They add Charlie's IP to a blacklist.
The company's database is never compromised because multiple security layers stopped the attack: Firewall blocked, IPS detected and blocked, Security team alerted.

security_lessons: Database port 3306 should never be open to the internet
IDS/IPS detects and blocks attack patterns
Security layers work together - even if one fails, others protect you

tracing_questions.question: In Scenario 1, why was the firewall able to let Google's response back into the network?
tracing_questions.answer: Because the firewall is stateful. It remembered that Alice made an outgoing connection to Google. When Google's response came back, the firewall recognized it as part of that connection and allowed it.

tracing_questions.question: In Scenario 2, why couldn't the hacker see Bob's data even if they intercepted the packets?
tracing_questions.answer: Because the VPN encrypted all data. Even if the hacker captured the packets, they would see only encrypted gibberish. Without the encryption key, they cannot decrypt and read the data.

tracing_questions.question: In Scenario 3, why should port 3306 (database) not be open to the internet?
tracing_questions.answer: Port 3306 is for database access. If it's open to the internet, any hacker can directly try to access the database. It should only be accessible from internal network or VPN users.

tracing_questions.question: If the company didn't have an IPS, what would happen in Scenario 3?
tracing_questions.answer: The IDS would still detect the attack and alert the security team, but the attack would continue until the team manually blocked it. With IPS, the attack is automatically stopped immediately.

units.title: Unit 4: Cryptography Essentials
units.description: Master how to protect data so only authorized people can read it

modules.title: Cryptography Essentials
modules.description: Master how to protect data so only authorized people can read it

topics.topic_name: Symmetric Encryption - AES
topics.explanation: Symmetric encryption means using the same key to both encrypt and decrypt data. It's like a lock where the same key locks and unlocks the door.

core_concept.what_it_is: One secret key is shared between two people. The sender uses the key to encrypt (lock) data. The receiver uses the same key to decrypt (unlock) data.
core_concept.formula: Plaintext (original message) + Encryption Key = Ciphertext (encrypted message). Ciphertext + Same Encryption Key = Plaintext (original message)

symmetric_analogy.analogy: You and your friend have identical keys to a safe. You put a message in the safe and lock it with your key. Your friend unlocks it with their identical key and reads the message.
symmetric_analogy.key_point: Both people must have the same key. If someone steals the key, they can both lock and unlock everything.

aes_encryption.what_is_aes: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the most widely used symmetric encryption algorithm. It's the gold standard for encryption.
aes_encryption.why_it_matters: AES is used by the US government, banks, and every major organization to protect classified and sensitive data.

aes_versions.strength: Strong - would take billions of years to crack with current computers
Very strong - even stronger than AES-128
Extremely strong - recommended for highly classified government data
aes_versions.use_case: Most secure encryption available. Used by NSA.

how_aes_works_conceptually.step1_substitution: Each character in the message is replaced with another character using the encryption key. Like a substitution cipher but with mathematical precision.
how_aes_works_conceptually.step2_permutation: The positions of characters are shuffled based on the key.
how_aes_works_conceptually.step3_mixing: Characters are mixed with the key multiple times (rounds). AES-128 uses 10 rounds, AES-256 uses 14 rounds.
how_aes_works_conceptually.step4_result: The plaintext is transformed into ciphertext that looks like random gibberish. Without the key, it's impossible to decrypt.
how_aes_works_conceptually.important: The details are complex mathematics, but the concept is simple: use the key to scramble data in a way that only someone with the key can unscramble it.

real_world_example.scenario: A bank encrypts customer account data at rest (stored on hard drives)
real_world_example.process: All customer data is encrypted using AES-256. The encryption key is stored in a secure Hardware Security Module (HSM). Even if someone steals the hard drive, the data is encrypted and useless without the key.
real_world_example.benefit: If a bank gets hacked, the attacker gets encrypted data, not readable customer information.

encryption_in_transit_example.process: Your message is encrypted using AES on your phone before being sent. It travels through the internet encrypted. Only the recipient's phone can decrypt it.
encryption_in_transit_example.result: WhatsApp, internet service providers, and hackers cannot see the message content - only encrypted gibberish.

advantages_of_symmetric.advantage: Very fast - encryption and decryption are quick
Uses less processing power than asymmetric encryption
advantages_of_symmetric.why: Suitable for encrypting large files and real-time communication

advantages_of_symmetric.advantage: Strong encryption - AES-256 is unbreakable with current technology
advantages_of_symmetric.why: Would take billions of years to brute force

disadvantages_of_symmetric.disadvantage: Key distribution problem - how do you securely share the key?
disadvantages_of_symmetric.challenge: If you send the key over the internet, an attacker can intercept it. Then both the key and the encrypted data are compromised.

disadvantages_of_symmetric.disadvantage: If the key is leaked, all encrypted data is compromised
disadvantages_of_symmetric.challenge: The same key encrypts and decrypts, so anyone with the key can read everything

disadvantages_of_symmetric.disadvantage: Not suitable for communication between strangers
disadvantages_of_symmetric.challenge: Two people need to meet in person or find a secure way to exchange the key first

topics.when_to_use_aes: Encrypting files on your computer, database encryption, encrypting data at rest, communication between organizations that already share a secure channel

topics.topic_name: Asymmetric Encryption - RSA
topics.explanation: Asymmetric encryption uses two different keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. Unlike symmetric, you don't need to share the decryption key.

core_concept.public_key: A key that is publicly shared. Anyone can use it to encrypt a message.
core_concept.private_key: A secret key that only you have. You use it to decrypt messages.
core_concept.unique_property: A message encrypted with the public key can ONLY be decrypted with the matching private key. The public key cannot decrypt data.

asymmetric_analogy.analogy: You have a mailbox in front of your house. Anyone (everyone has the public key) can drop a letter into your mailbox. But only you (with the private key) can open the mailbox and read the letters.
asymmetric_analogy.advantage: Strangers don't need a shared secret key to send you encrypted messages.

rsa_encryption.what_is_rsa: RSA is the most common asymmetric encryption algorithm. It's named after its inventors: Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman.

rsa_key_sizes.strength: Weak - can be cracked with modern computers

how_rsa_works_conceptually.step1_key_generation: A large number is generated (product of two large prime numbers). This creates both public and private keys mathematically linked.
how_rsa_works_conceptually.step2_key_pair: Public key = can be shared with the world. Private key = must be kept secret.
how_rsa_works_conceptually.step3_encryption: Someone encrypts a message with your public key. The encrypted message can only be decrypted with your private key.
how_rsa_works_conceptually.step4_decryption: You decrypt the message with your private key. Only you can read it.
how_rsa_works_conceptually.mathematical_principle: It's mathematically easy to encrypt with the public key, but nearly impossible to decrypt without the private key. This is based on the difficulty of factoring large prime numbers.

real_world_example.scenario: Sending a secure email to a bank
process: The bank publishes its public key on their website
You download the bank's public key
You type your sensitive information and encrypt it with the bank's public key
The encrypted message is sent over the internet
Even if a hacker intercepts it, they only have the encrypted message and the public key. They cannot decrypt it.
The bank receives the message and decrypts it with their private key (which only they have)
Only the bank can read your sensitive information
A software company creates a new version of their antivirus software
They encrypt the software file with their private key (creates a digital signature - covered later)
Users download the software
Users can decrypt with the company's public key to verify the software is authentic and hasn't been modified
If the decryption fails, the software is fake or modified by a hacker

rsa_vs_aes.comparison: Asymmetric (RSA) is used to securely exchange symmetric (AES) keys. RSA encrypts the AES key, then AES encrypts the actual data. Best of both worlds.

topics.when_to_use_rsa: HTTPS/TLS connections, email encryption, digital signatures, secure key exchange, communicating with people you haven't met before

topics.topic_name: Hashing - MD5, SHA-256, and Why It's Different
topics.explanation: Hashing is NOT encryption. A hash function converts any data into a fixed-size string of characters. The process is one-way - you cannot reverse it to get the original data.

key_difference_from_encryption.encryption: Reversible - with the key, you can get the original plaintext back
key_difference_from_encryption.hashing: Irreversible - there is no key. You cannot get the original data back from a hash

hashing_analogy.analogy: Imagine a food blender. You put an apple into a blender and get apple juice. You cannot put the juice back together to get the apple. The apple is gone. Hashing works the same way - data goes in, a hash comes out, and you cannot reverse it.
hashing_analogy.purpose: Hashing is not about hiding data. It's about creating a unique fingerprint of data to detect changes.

how_hash_functions_work.step1: Input: Any data (text, file, image, video) of any size
how_hash_functions_work.step2: Process: Run through a mathematical algorithm
how_hash_functions_work.step3: output: Fixed-size string of characters called a hash or digest

hash_properties.what_it_means: Same input always produces the same hash
hash_properties.example: 'Hello' always produces the same SHA-256 hash

hash_properties.what_it_means: Can hash large files in seconds
hash_properties.example: Hash a 1GB file in less than a second

hash_properties.what_it_means: Cannot get the original data from the hash
hash_properties.example: SHA-256 hash cannot be reversed - it's one-way

hash_properties.what_it_means: Changing even one character changes the entire hash
Nearly impossible to find two different inputs with the same hash
hash_properties.example: Finding two different messages with the same SHA-256 hash is computationally impossible

common_hash_algorithms.status: BROKEN - should not use for security
common_hash_algorithms.why_broken: Collisions have been found. Two different files can have the same MD5 hash.
common_hash_algorithms.current_use: Checksums for files (non-security), legacy systems only

common_hash_algorithms.why_deprecated: Theoretical attacks exist. Collisions are close to being practical.
common_hash_algorithms.current_use: Some legacy systems, but being replaced
Bitcoin, passwords, digital signatures, SSL certificates

common_hash_algorithms.why_good: Latest standard. More resistant to future attacks than SHA-2.

real_world_use_case_1_password_storage.wrong_way: Store plaintext passwords in database. If database is hacked, all passwords are exposed.
real_world_use_case_1_password_storage.right_way: Hash each password using SHA-256. Store only the hash. When user logs in, hash their input and compare with stored hash.
example: Website hashes it: SHA-256('MyPassword123') = abc123xyz (not the real hash, simplified)
When user logs in, they enter 'MyPassword123'
Website hashes the input: SHA-256('MyPassword123') = abc123xyz
If database is hacked, attacker gets 'abc123xyz' but cannot reverse it to get 'MyPassword123'
real_world_use_case_1_password_storage.additional_security: Websites use salting and key derivation functions (like bcrypt, PBKDF2) which add extra layers to make cracking even harder

real_world_use_case_2_file_integrity.scenario: Downloading a large software file from the internet
real_world_use_case_2_file_integrity.problem: During transfer, the file might get corrupted. Or a hacker might modify it.
real_world_use_case_2_file_integrity.solution: The website publishes the file's SHA-256 hash. After downloading, you hash the file and compare.
example: You open terminal and run: sha256sum ubuntu.iso
If your hash matches the published hash, the file is unmodified and authentic
If it doesn't match, the file was corrupted or modified by a hacker

real_world_use_case_3_blockchain.scenario: Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies use hashing
real_world_use_case_3_blockchain.how_it_works: Each block in the blockchain contains a hash of the previous block. If someone tries to modify an old transaction, the hash changes, breaking the chain.
real_world_use_case_3_blockchain.security: This makes Bitcoin's ledger immutable - you cannot secretly change past transactions without breaking the entire blockchain

why_hashing_is_different_from_encryption.encryption: Hide data so only authorized people can read it
why_hashing_is_different_from_encryption.hashing: Detect if data has been changed
Much faster - can hash huge files instantly

topics.remember: Hashing is for integrity checking. Encryption is for keeping secrets. They serve different purposes and are not interchangeable.

topics.topic_name: Digital Signatures - Authentication and Non-repudiation
topics.explanation: A digital signature proves that you created or approved a document. It's like your handwritten signature on a paper contract, but for digital documents.

what_digital_signature_does.what_it_proves: Proves who created or approved the document
what_digital_signature_does.example: A bank digitally signs a loan approval. You know it came from the real bank, not a forged email.

what_digital_signature_does.what_it_proves: The signer cannot deny they signed it later
what_digital_signature_does.example: If you digitally sign a contract, you cannot later claim 'I never signed this'. The signature proves you did.

what_digital_signature_does.what_it_proves: The document has not been modified after signing
what_digital_signature_does.example: If someone changes a word in a contract after you signed it, the signature becomes invalid.

how_digital_signatures_work.step1: Document creation: You have a document to sign (email, contract, software update)
how_digital_signatures_work.step2: Hashing: The document is hashed using SHA-256. This creates a unique fingerprint.
how_digital_signatures_work.step3: Encryption: The hash is encrypted with your private key. This encrypted hash is the 'digital signature'.
how_digital_signatures_work.step4: Attachment: The signature is attached to the document and sent.
how_digital_signatures_work.step5_verification: Recipient decrypts the signature with your public key to get the hash.
how_digital_signatures_work.step6_verification: Recipient hashes the document themselves and compares with the decrypted hash.
how_digital_signatures_work.step7_verification: If hashes match, the signature is valid. Document is authentic and unchanged.
how_digital_signatures_work.step8_verification: If hashes don't match, someone modified the document after signing, or the signature is forged.

digital_signature_analogy.analogy: You write a letter and sign it with a special ink that only you can produce. The recipient shines a light on the signature and sees a unique pattern that proves only you could have created it. If the letter's content is changed, the ink pattern changes and no longer matches.
digital_signature_analogy.key_difference: Digital signatures use mathematics instead of ink, and are absolutely impossible to forge if the private key is secure.

why_this_uses_both_hashing_and_encryptio.purpose: Creates a small fingerprint of the entire document. Even large files produce a small hash.
Encrypts only the hash with private key, proving you approved it. If we encrypted the entire document, it would be slow.

why_this_uses_both_hashing_and_encryptio.benefit: Efficiency: You only encrypt a small hash, not the entire document

process: You write: 'Please approve the $1 million budget transfer'
You digitally sign the email with your private key
Email is sent to your boss
Your boss verifies the signature using your public key
If valid, your boss knows: (1) It came from you, (2) The email content hasn't been modified, (3) You cannot deny writing it later
Microsoft hashes the update file
Microsoft signs the hash with their private key
The signed update is published online
When you download it, your computer verifies the signature using Microsoft's public key
If valid, you know: (1) It's from the real Microsoft, (2) It hasn't been modified by hackers
If invalid, your computer rejects it - it's fake malware or corrupted

legal_importance.in_many_countries: Digital signatures are legally binding and equivalent to handwritten signatures
legal_importance.use_cases: Contracts, financial transactions, government documents, legal agreements
legal_importance.requirement: The private key must be kept secret and secure. If someone steals your private key, they can forge your signature.

common_digital_signature_standards.how_it_works: Using RSA encryption to sign the hash
Using elliptic curve cryptography to sign
common_digital_signature_standards.advantage: Faster and uses smaller keys than RSA
More efficient and secure than ECDSA

topics.topic_name: SSL/TLS - HTTPS and Secure Web Communication
topics.explanation: SSL/TLS is a protocol that encrypts communication between your browser and a website. When you see the padlock icon on a website, that's SSL/TLS at work.

ssl_vs_tls.ssl_history: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was the original protocol created in the 1990s
ssl_vs_tls.ssl_status: Deprecated - no longer used. Has known security vulnerabilities.
ssl_vs_tls.tls_history: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the modern replacement for SSL
ssl_vs_tls.tls_status: Current standard. TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are widely used.
ssl_vs_tls.common_terminology: People still call it 'SSL' informally, but they usually mean TLS

what_ssl_tls_protects.what_it_means: Your data is encrypted between your browser and the website
what_ssl_tls_protects.example: Your password is encrypted. Hackers on the WiFi cannot see it in plaintext.

what_ssl_tls_protects.what_it_means: Data cannot be modified in transit
what_ssl_tls_protects.example: A hacker cannot change the price of an item on a shopping site.

what_ssl_tls_protects.what_it_means: The website is who it claims to be
what_ssl_tls_protects.example: You're sure you're talking to the real Amazon, not a fake website.

how_https_works.step2_certificate: Amazon's server sends its SSL certificate (contains Amazon's public key and proof of identity)
how_https_works.step3_verification: Your browser verifies the certificate: Is it signed by a trusted Certificate Authority? Is the domain correct? Has it expired?
how_https_works.step4_key_exchange: Your browser generates a random session key (symmetric key). It encrypts this key with Amazon's public key and sends it.
how_https_works.step5_shared_secret: Amazon decrypts with their private key and gets the session key. Now both have the same symmetric key.
how_https_works.step6_encryption: All further communication is encrypted using the session key (AES)
how_https_works.step7_security: Even if a hacker intercepts packets, they only see encrypted gibberish

ssl_certificate.what_it_is: A digital file that contains: Website's public key, Website's domain name, Certificate validity period, Certificate Authority's digital signature
ssl_certificate.who_issues_it: Certificate Authorities (CA) like DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Symantec. These are trusted organizations.
ssl_certificate.how_it_proves_identity: The CA verifies that you actually own the domain before issuing the certificate. They sign it with their private key, proving it's authentic.
ssl_certificate.trust_chain: Your browser trusts major CAs. If a certificate is signed by a trusted CA, your browser trusts the website.

https_vs_http.http: No encryption. Data visible to anyone on the network. Old and insecure.
https_vs_http.https: Encryption via SSL/TLS. Data encrypted. Modern and secure.
https_vs_http.visual_indicator: Your browser shows a padlock icon for HTTPS. No padlock or a warning icon means HTTP or invalid certificate.

simplified_summary: Client Hello: Browser sends list of supported encryption algorithms and random number
Server Hello: Server picks one algorithm, sends certificate and another random number
Key Exchange: Browser and server generate a shared session key
Finished: Both sides verify they derived the same key correctly
Communication: All data is now encrypted with the session key

perfect_forward_secrecy.what_it_is: Even if a server's private key is stolen in the future, past conversations cannot be decrypted
perfect_forward_secrecy.how_it_works: Session keys are generated fresh for each connection and deleted after use. Past session keys are never stored.
perfect_forward_secrecy.importance: Even if an attacker hacks the server and steals the private key today, they cannot decrypt old conversations from the past

real_world_example.scenario: Logging into your bank account on public WiFi
real_world_example.with_http: Your password is sent in plaintext. A hacker on the WiFi captures it immediately. They access your bank account.
real_world_example.with_https: Your password is encrypted with SSL/TLS. Hacker on WiFi sees only encrypted gibberish. Cannot read your password. Your account is safe.

certificate_pinning.advanced_concept: Some apps (like banking apps) 'pin' the expected certificate. If the certificate changes, the app rejects it.
certificate_pinning.protects_against: Man-in-the-middle attacks where an attacker intercepts traffic and presents a different certificate
certificate_pinning.implementation: Banks and critical services use this for extra security

tls_versions.reason: Vulnerable to POODLE and other attacks
Good security. Still used on many websites.
Faster handshake, better security, removed obsolete algorithms

topics.topic_name: Key Management - Generating, Storing, and Rotating Keys Safely
topics.explanation: Keys are the foundation of cryptography. If keys are compromised or poorly managed, all encryption is useless. Key management is critical.

key_management_principles.what_it_means: Keys must be generated using cryptographically secure random sources
key_management_principles.example: Do NOT use weak random generators. Use /dev/urandom on Linux or CryptographicRandomNumberGenerator in .NET

key_management_principles.what_it_means: Keys must be stored securely, not in plaintext
key_management_principles.example: Store private keys in encrypted files, HSMs (Hardware Security Modules), or key vaults

key_management_principles.what_it_means: Only authorized people can access the key
key_management_principles.example: Use multi-factor authentication to access keys. Log all access.

key_management_principles.what_it_means: Replace old keys with new ones periodically
key_management_principles.example: Change encryption keys every year. If a key is compromised, only data encrypted with that key is at risk.

key_management_principles.what_it_means: Have secure backups in case a key is lost
key_management_principles.example: Store backup keys in a secure location separate from the original
When a key is retired, overwrite it multiple times or burn it if it's on physical media

symmetric_key_generation.what_to_do: Use a cryptographically secure random number generator to create a random key
symmetric_key_generation.example: Generate 256 random bits for AES-256 key

asymmetric_key_generation.what_to_do: Use established tools like OpenSSL to generate RSA or ECDSA key pairs

key_generation.common_mistake: Using weak random sources like rand() function in programming languages. This is not cryptographically secure.

key_storage_options.security: Very low - key is readable if file is accessed
Medium - file is encrypted, but password to decrypt it might be weak
key_storage_options.use_case: Acceptable for development, not for production

key_storage_options.security: Low-Medium - variables visible in logs and process lists
High - centralized, access controlled, audited, rotated automatically
key_storage_options.examples: Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault

key_storage_options.security: Very high - physical device, key never leaves the device

hardware_security_module_hsm.what_is_hsm: A physical device that stores and manages cryptographic keys. The key never leaves the device.
hardware_security_module_hsm.why_its_important: Even if someone steals the HSM, they cannot extract the key without the PIN/password.
hardware_security_module_hsm.how_it_works: Your application sends data to the HSM. The HSM encrypts or decrypts it and returns the result. The key stays inside the HSM.
hardware_security_module_hsm.real_world_use: Banks, government agencies, cloud providers protecting their encryption keys
hardware_security_module_hsm.example: AWS CloudHSM - encrypted key storage in cloud with hardware protection

key_rotation.what_it_is: Periodically creating new keys and re-encrypting data with them
key_rotation.why_it_matters: If an old key is compromised, rotation limits the amount of data at risk
how_it_works: Create a new encryption key
Re-encrypt all data encrypted with the old key using the new key
Keep the old key for a while (to decrypt old data if needed)
Eventually retire and destroy the old key
key_rotation.rotation_schedule: Annual rotation for most organizations. More frequent for very sensitive data.

key_derivation.what_it_is: Creating multiple keys from a single master key or password
key_derivation.why_useful: If one key is compromised, other keys derived from the same master are not affected (if using proper techniques)
key_derivation.example: PBKDF2, bcrypt - derive a strong encryption key from a user's password

key_escrow_and_key_recovery.key_escrow: A trusted third party holds a backup of the key in case the owner loses it
key_escrow_and_key_recovery.use_case: Employee leaves company and their private key needs to be accessed
key_escrow_and_key_recovery.controversy: Government agencies request key escrow for law enforcement access (controversial privacy issue)

common_key_management_mistakes.consequence: If code is leaked, all keys are exposed

common_key_management_mistakes.mistake: Using the same key for everything
common_key_management_mistakes.consequence: Compromise of one key means everything is compromised
Cannot audit who used the key. Cannot revoke individual access.
Compromise of a key could have been done long ago and go undetected
If database is hacked, keys are exposed

units.title: Unit 5: Web Application Security
units.description: Learn how to identify and prevent the most common attacks on web applications

modules.title: Web Application Security
modules.description: Learn how to identify and prevent the most common attacks on web applications

topics.topic_name: OWASP Top 10 - The Most Critical Web Vulnerabilities
topics.explanation: OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) is an organization that publishes the most dangerous web application vulnerabilities. The Top 10 list changes every few years based on real-world attacks.
topics.what_is_owasp: OWASP is a non-profit organization focused on improving software security. Their Top 10 list is the industry standard for web application security.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Users can access data or perform actions they shouldn't be allowed to
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: You change the URL from /user/profile/123 to /user/profile/456 and can see another user's private information
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: A user can edit other users' orders or profiles just by changing IDs in the URL
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Always check if the user is authorized before showing data. Never trust user input to determine what data to show.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Sensitive data is not properly encrypted or protected
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: A website stores passwords in plaintext instead of hashing them. Database gets hacked and all passwords are exposed.
