current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Attackers steal unencrypted credit cards, health records, or personal data from the database
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Encrypt sensitive data in transit (HTTPS) and at rest (encryption in database). Use strong hashing for passwords.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Attacker inserts malicious code into input fields which gets executed
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: A login form vulnerable to SQL injection. Entering ' OR '1'='1' bypasses password check.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Use prepared statements (parameterized queries). Never concatenate user input into SQL commands.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Security is not built into the design from the start. Security is an afterthought.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: An app has no rate limiting. Attacker can brute-force passwords with thousands of attempts per minute.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Password reset links don't expire. Attacker intercepts email and resets password even days later.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Security should be planned from the beginning. Include threat modeling during design phase.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Default settings, debug features, or unnecessary services left enabled on production servers
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: Admin console is accessible without authentication. Default password is never changed.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Attacker accesses admin dashboard with default credentials like admin:admin
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Change all default passwords. Disable unnecessary features. Keep servers updated.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Using libraries and frameworks with known security vulnerabilities
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: Website uses jQuery version 1.9 from 2013 which has 50+ known vulnerabilities
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Attacker exploits a known vulnerability in an old library to inject code
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Keep all dependencies updated. Use tools to scan for vulnerable libraries.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Weak authentication mechanisms that can be bypassed or brute-forced
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: No account lockout after failed login attempts. Password is only 4 characters. No multi-factor authentication.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Attacker tries 100,000 password combinations. Account gets hacked.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Use strong authentication: MFA, account lockout, password requirements, secure session management.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Code or data can be modified by unauthorized parties during transfer or update
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: Mobile app updates are not digitally signed. Attacker distributes fake app with malware.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: CI/CD pipeline is compromised and malicious code is deployed to production
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Use digital signatures. Verify integrity of updates. Secure CI/CD pipeline.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Security events are not logged or monitored, so attacks go undetected
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: Successful login after 1000 failed attempts is not logged. Nobody knows the account was compromised.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Attackers modify or delete logs after breaking in to cover their tracks
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Log all security events. Monitor logs for suspicious activity. Store logs securely with immutability.

current_owasp_top_10_2024.what_it_is: Attacker tricks the server into making requests to internal systems
current_owasp_top_10_2024.example: Image upload feature accepts URLs. Attacker provides: http://192.168.1.1/admin (internal IP). Server downloads from internal network.
current_owasp_top_10_2024.real_attack: Attacker accesses internal services, cloud metadata APIs, or private databases
current_owasp_top_10_2024.prevention: Validate and whitelist URLs. Don't allow requests to internal IPs. Use proper network segmentation.

topics.topic_name: SQL Injection - Most Common and Dangerous
topics.explanation: SQL injection is when an attacker inserts malicious SQL code into input fields. It's the most common web vulnerability because it's easy to exploit and very dangerous.

how_sql_injection_works.normal_sql: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' AND password='password123'

malicious_injection_example.resulting_sql: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='' OR '1'='1' AND password='anything'
malicious_injection_example.what_happens: The condition '1'='1' is always true, so the query returns all users without checking password
malicious_injection_example.result: Attacker logs in as the first user (usually admin) without knowing the password

more_dangerous_injection.resulting_sql: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='' OR '1'='1'; DROP TABLE users; -- AND password='anything'
more_dangerous_injection.what_happens: First query returns all users, then the entire users table is deleted. The -- comments out the rest of the SQL.
more_dangerous_injection.damage: All user data is destroyed. Complete data loss.

injection_variations.how_it_works: Attacker enters code that returns true or false to extract data one character at a time
injection_variations.example: ' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE username='admin') = 'a' --

injection_variations.how_it_works: Attacker enters code that causes database to delay if condition is true
injection_variations.example: '; IF (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users) > 5 WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:10'--

injection_variations.how_it_works: Attacker adds UNION SELECT to combine results from another table
injection_variations.example: ' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users --

injection_variations.how_it_works: Attacker adds semicolon to execute multiple SQL statements
injection_variations.example: '; UPDATE users SET admin=1 WHERE username='hacker'; --

real_world_sql_injection_attacks.damage: 100,000 user accounts exposed, stolen data sold on black market
147 million people's personal data exposed (credit cards, SSNs, birthdays)
4 million customers' data stolen, company fined

how_to_prevent_sql_injection.what_it_is: Code template separates SQL logic from data. Data is treated as pure data, never as code.
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.example_vulnerable: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='" + username + "'"
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.example_safe: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=?"; query.bind(username);
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.why_it_works: The database knows that username is data, not code. Even if it contains SQL keywords, they're treated as strings.

how_to_prevent_sql_injection.what_it_is: Check that input matches expected format before using it
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.example: If expecting a number, reject non-numeric input. If expecting email, validate email format.

how_to_prevent_sql_injection.what_it_is: Replace dangerous characters with safe versions
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.example: Replace ' with \'. But parameterized queries are better.

how_to_prevent_sql_injection.what_it_is: Libraries like Hibernate or Sequelize automatically use parameterized queries
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.benefit: Programmer doesn't have to manually write safe SQL

how_to_prevent_sql_injection.what_it_is: Database user has only necessary permissions
how_to_prevent_sql_injection.example: Webapp database user can only SELECT, not DROP or UPDATE. If SQL injection occurs, damage is limited.

topics.topic_name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) - Running Malicious JavaScript
topics.explanation: XSS is when an attacker injects malicious JavaScript code into a web application. The browser then executes this code, stealing cookies, redirecting users, or defacing the page.

how_xss_works.scenario: A social media app lets users write comments. No input validation.
how_xss_works.what_happens: The comment is stored in the database as HTML
how_xss_works.when_others_view: Their browser sees the HTML, interprets the <script> tag, and executes the JavaScript
how_xss_works.result: All users who view this comment see the alert box

more_dangerous_xss.what_it_does: Sends the user's session cookie to the attacker's server
more_dangerous_xss.impact: Attacker receives cookies containing session tokens, can now impersonate that user

types_of_xss.what_it_is: Malicious code is stored in the database and executed every time someone views it
types_of_xss.example: Comment on social media with JavaScript. Every time someone visits your profile, the script runs.

types_of_xss.what_it_is: Malicious code is in the URL and executed when someone visits that specific link
types_of_xss.example: URL with malicious query parameter. Only the person who clicks this link is affected.
types_of_xss.danger_level: Medium - requires user to click a link

types_of_xss.what_it_is: Malicious code executes in the browser by modifying the DOM (page structure)
types_of_xss.example: JavaScript code uses unsanitized URL parameters to modify the page
types_of_xss.danger_level: High - happens entirely in the browser

xss_attack_examples.impact: Attacker gets your session, can log in as you
Attacker records every key you type on that site
Page shows fake login form, collects username and password
User is redirected to a malware site

how_to_prevent_xss.example: If expecting a comment, reject input containing <script> tags

how_to_prevent_xss.what_it_is: Convert dangerous characters to safe HTML entities
how_to_prevent_xss.result: <script> is displayed as text, not executed as code

how_to_prevent_xss.what_it_is: HTTP header that restricts what scripts can run on a page
how_to_prevent_xss.example: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' (only scripts from the same domain are allowed)
how_to_prevent_xss.benefit: Even if malicious script is injected, browser refuses to execute it

how_to_prevent_xss.what_it_is: Modern web frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) automatically escape output by default
how_to_prevent_xss.example: React automatically escapes user input so XSS is prevented

how_to_prevent_xss.what_it_is: All user input is potentially malicious until validated and escaped
how_to_prevent_xss.principle: Sanitize on input, escape on output

topics.topic_name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
topics.explanation: CSRF tricks users into performing unwanted actions on a website where they're already logged in. The attacker doesn't see the response, but the action is performed.

how_csrf_works.scenario: You're logged into your bank account in one browser tab
how_csrf_works.attacker_trick: You click a link to another website in a different tab (attacker's site)
how_csrf_works.what_happens: Your browser automatically includes your bank cookies when loading this image
how_csrf_works.result: Bank processes the transfer because your session is valid. You didn't intend to transfer, but it happened.

real_world_example.scenario: Popular forum has CSRF vulnerability in 'change email' form
real_world_example.result: Any logged-in user who views the post has their email changed to attacker's email
real_world_example.impact: Attacker can now reset passwords and take over accounts

csrf_vs_xss.xss: Attacker injects code that runs in victim's browser. Attacker can see responses.
csrf_vs_xss.csrf: Attacker tricks victim's browser into making a request. Attacker cannot see responses, but request is processed by the server.

how_to_prevent_csrf.what_it_is: Server generates a unique token and includes it in every form. Token is checked on submission.
how_it_works: Server creates a unique token: xyz789abc123
Token is included in form: <input type='hidden' name='csrf_token' value='xyz789abc123'>
When form is submitted, token is sent to server
Server checks: Is token valid and matches the session? If yes, process request. If no, reject.
how_to_prevent_csrf.why_it_works: Attacker's website doesn't have the token (it's unique per session and server won't reveal it). So CSRF request fails.

how_to_prevent_csrf.what_it_is: Browser setting that prevents cookies from being sent with cross-site requests
how_to_prevent_csrf.result: Cookie is only sent when request comes from your own website, not from attacker's site

how_to_prevent_csrf.what_it_is: Cookies and request headers must match
how_to_prevent_csrf.example: Token is in cookie AND in request header. Server checks they match.

how_to_prevent_csrf.what_it_is: Server checks that request came from your own website
how_to_prevent_csrf.limitation: Referer can be spoofed in some cases. Not reliable alone.

topics.topic_name: Input Validation and Sanitization
topics.explanation: Input validation checks that user input is in the correct format and safe before using it. Sanitization removes dangerous characters or code.

input_validation_basics.what_it_is: Checking that input meets expected criteria before processing it
input_validation_basics.principle: Never trust user input. Validate everything.

validation_types.check: Is input the correct data type?
validation_types.example: Age should be a number, not text. Email should contain @
Username between 3-20 characters. Password at least 8 characters.

validation_types.check: Is input from a list of allowed values?
validation_types.example: Country must be one of: USA, Canada, Mexico. Not any random string.

validation_vs_sanitization.validation: Rejects invalid input. If invalid, asks user to correct it.
validation_vs_sanitization.sanitization: Removes or escapes dangerous parts of input, but keeps the rest.

sanitization_techniques.what_it_does: Converts HTML special characters to safe entities
sanitization_techniques.result: HTML code is displayed as text, not interpreted

sanitization_techniques.what_it_does: Converts special characters to URL-safe format
sanitization_techniques.use: When including user input in URLs

sanitization_techniques.what_it_does: Escapes quotes and special characters for SQL
Escapes quotes and special characters for JavaScript
sanitization_techniques.use: When putting user input in JavaScript code

sanitization_techniques.what_it_does: Removes all HTML and script tags from input

blacklist_approach.what_it_is: Define dangerous patterns and reject them
blacklist_approach.example: Reject input containing: <script>, SELECT, DROP, etc.
blacklist_approach.problem: Attackers can bypass with encoding tricks. New attacks emerge. Never complete.

whitelist_approach.what_it_is: Define allowed patterns and accept ONLY those
whitelist_approach.example: Username can only contain letters, numbers, underscore. Everything else is rejected.
whitelist_approach.advantage: More secure. Doesn't matter what new attacks exist - if it doesn't match whitelist, rejected.

username_validation: Whitelist: Only alphanumeric and underscore (a-z, A-Z, 0-9, _)
Not in list of reserved names (admin, root, system)
If validation fails: Show error 'Username can only contain letters, numbers, underscore'
email_validation: Check format using regex pattern for valid emails
Verify email by sending confirmation link
If validation fails: Show error 'Please enter a valid email address'
password_validation: Must contain uppercase, lowercase, number, and symbol
Hash and store in database (don't store plaintext)

topics.topic_name: Authentication vs. Authorization
topics.explanation: Authentication proves WHO you are. Authorization determines WHAT you can do. Both are critical but different.

authentication_basics.what_it_is: Proving your identity. The process of verifying 'You are who you claim to be'
authentication_basics.real_world_analogy: Showing your passport at border control. The officer checks: Is this your passport? Is it valid? Are you the person in the photo?

methods.how: You enter a password. System checks if it matches stored hash.
Password + SMS code or Authenticator app or Biometric
methods.security: Strong - even if password is stolen, account is safe
Very strong - nearly impossible to hack

authorization_basics.what_it_is: Determining what an authenticated user can do. The process of verifying 'You are allowed to access this resource'
authorization_basics.real_world_analogy: After border officer verifies your identity, they check: Are you allowed to enter this country? Do you have a visa? Are you on the watch list?

methods.how: User is assigned a role (admin, user, moderator). Each role has specific permissions.
methods.example: Admin can delete users. Moderator can delete comments. User can only delete their own posts.

methods.how: Access decisions based on attributes: user attributes, resource attributes, environment attributes
methods.example: Allow access if: user.department == 'finance' AND resource.classification == 'public' AND time < 18:00

methods.how: For each resource, specify which users/roles can access it
methods.example: File document.pdf: Owner (read, write, delete), HR department (read), Everyone else (none)

authentication_failures.what_happens: Users can set simple passwords like '123456' that are easy to brute-force
authentication_failures.fix: Require strong passwords: 12+ characters, mix of uppercase, lowercase, numbers, symbols

authentication_failures.what_happens: Attacker tries unlimited password combinations. No limit on attempts.
authentication_failures.fix: Lock account after 5-10 failed attempts for 30 minutes

authentication_failures.what_happens: Attacker knows session ID before user logs in. After user logs in, attacker uses same ID.
authentication_failures.fix: Generate new session ID after successful login

authentication_failures.what_happens: If database is hacked, all passwords are immediately usable
authentication_failures.fix: Hash passwords using bcrypt, PBKDF2, or Argon2

authentication_failures.what_happens: If password is stolen, attacker has full access

authorization_failures.what_happens: User can access resources they shouldn't. Example: Edit URL from /profile/123 to /profile/456 and see other user's data
authorization_failures.fix: Always check authorization before showing data. Verify user owns the resource.

authorization_failures.what_happens: Regular user can become admin by modifying request: user.role = 'admin' in local storage
authorization_failures.fix: Never trust client-side role. Always verify role on server-side.

authorization_failures.what_happens: User A can see User B's data by changing their own user ID in the request
authorization_failures.fix: Always verify user owns the resource before returning it

authorization_failures.what_happens: Regular user performs admin functions by directly accessing admin endpoints
authorization_failures.fix: Check authorization for EVERY endpoint, not just obvious admin pages

proper_implementation.step1: Authentication: Verify user identity (login with password + MFA)
proper_implementation.step2: Generate Session: Create session token/JWT and store on client
proper_implementation.step3: Authorization Check: For EVERY request, verify user is authenticated
proper_implementation.step4: Permission Check: Verify user has permission for this specific action
proper_implementation.step5: Grant Access: If all checks pass, proceed with request
proper_implementation.step6: Log Access: Log who accessed what for audit trail

topics.topic_name: Session Management - Tokens, Cookies, and Secure Storage
topics.explanation: After a user logs in, the server must remember they're logged in. Sessions manage this memory. Improper session management is a critical vulnerability.

session_basics.what_is_a_session: A period during which a user is logged into the application
session_basics.why_needed: HTTP is stateless - server doesn't remember previous requests. Sessions create continuity.
session_basics.analogy: At a restaurant, when you order, the waiter needs to remember which table is yours. Sessions are like the waiter remembering which table ordered what.

how_it_works: User logs in with username and password
Server creates a session ID (random, unique string)
Server stores session data in memory or database with all user information
Server sends session ID to client via cookie
Client automatically includes cookie in every request
Server looks up session ID, retrieves user data
advantages: Server has full control - can revoke session immediately
User data is not exposed on client
Can store large amounts of data
disadvantages: Requires database/memory to store all sessions
Doesn't scale well across multiple servers
Sessions are lost if server restarts

how_it_works: User logs in
Server creates a JWT containing user information
Server signs JWT with secret key to prevent tampering
Server sends JWT to client
Client stores JWT in local or session storage
Client includes JWT in every request
Server verifies JWT signature and checks expiration
advantages: Scalable - no database needed for session lookup
Stateless - server doesn't need to remember anything
disadvantages: If secret key is compromised, all tokens are compromised

cookies.what_is_cookie: A small file stored on client that browser automatically sends with requests
how_it_works: Server sends: Set-Cookie: sessionID=abc123
Browser stores this cookie
On next request to same domain, browser includes: Cookie: sessionID=abc123

cookie_attributes.what_it_does: Prevents JavaScript from accessing cookie (only sent in HTTP requests)
cookie_attributes.security_benefit: Protects against XSS attacks stealing the cookie

cookie_attributes.what_it_does: Cookie is only sent over HTTPS, not HTTP
cookie_attributes.security_benefit: Prevents man-in-the-middle attacks from stealing unencrypted cookie

cookie_attributes.strict: Cookie never sent with cross-site requests (prevents CSRF)
cookie_attributes.lax: Cookie sent with top-level navigation but not embedded requests
cookie_attributes.none: Cookie sent with all requests (requires Secure attribute)

cookie_attributes.example: Max-Age=3600 means cookie expires in 1 hour

cookie_attributes.what_it_does: Which domains can access this cookie
cookie_attributes.example: Domain=example.com means cookie sent to example.com and subdomains

where_to_store_session.option1: Cookie with HttpOnly + Secure flags (safest for traditional sessions)
where_to_store_session.option3: sessionStorage (deleted when browser closes, but still risky)
where_to_store_session.recommendation: Use HttpOnly cookies for authentication tokens

session_security_practices.what_it_means: Use cryptographically secure random generator, not basic random
session_security_practices.why: Weak random can be predicted by attacker

session_security_practices.what_it_means: Sessions expire after period of inactivity
session_security_practices.example: 30 minutes of no activity = automatic logout
session_security_practices.benefit: Prevents unauthorized access if user leaves device unattended

session_security_practices.what_it_means: Session expires after X hours regardless of activity
session_security_practices.example: 8-hour work shift - session expires after 8 hours even if active
session_security_practices.benefit: Limits damage if session is stolen

session_security_practices.what_it_means: Create new session ID after successful authentication
Delete session from server when user logs out
session_security_practices.why: Prevents reuse of old session IDs

session_security_practices.what_it_means: Monitor for unusual activity: IP change, User-Agent change, multiple simultaneous sessions
session_security_practices.action: Log user out and require re-authentication

jwt_security_practices.benefit: If token is stolen, it's only valid briefly

jwt_security_practices.what_it_means: Use short-lived access token plus longer-lived refresh token
jwt_security_practices.how: When access token expires, use refresh token to get new access token
jwt_security_practices.benefit: Access token can be short-lived, reducing exposure if stolen

jwt_security_practices.when: When user logs out or changes password
jwt_security_practices.limitation: Requires database, defeats the 'stateless' advantage of JWT

jwt_security_practices.what_it_means: Send JWT as HttpOnly cookie, not localStorage

topics.topic_name: API Security - Rate Limiting, Token-Based Auth, OAuth and JWT
topics.explanation: APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) are programs that communicate with other programs. Securing APIs is critical because they often handle sensitive operations and data.

api_security_importance.why_apis_need_security: APIs often don't have a human user interface, so traditional security measures don't apply
api_security_importance.common_targets: APIs are primary targets for attackers - they automate attacks and access data at scale
api_security_importance.examples: Banking APIs, social media APIs, payment APIs

rate_limiting.what_it_is: Limiting how many requests a user/IP can make in a time period

why_it_matters.example: Attacker tries 100,000 passwords per minute. Rate limiting stops this.
Attacker sends millions of requests to overload server. Rate limiting prevents this.
Attacker continuously calls API to copy all data. Rate limiting prevents this.

implementation_examples.effect: IP address exceeding 100 requests/minute gets error response
Authenticated user exceeding 1000 requests/hour is blocked

token_based_authentication.what_it_is: API uses tokens instead of passwords for authentication
why_better_than_passwords: Passwords sent in plain request are exposed to anyone
flow: User provides username and password (once, securely)
User includes token in every API request
Server validates token and processes request

oauth_2_0.what_is_oauth: Protocol for delegated access. Third-party apps can access your data without having your password.
oauth_2_0.real_world_example: Sign up to a website using 'Sign in with Google'. Google grants the website permission to access your profile without ever sharing your Google password.
why_it_matters: You don't share password with third-party apps
More secure than giving password to every app
oauth_flow: You log in to Google and grant permission
Google redirects back to website with a token
Website uses token to access your Google data
You're now logged in without sharing password with website

oauth_roles.who: The website trying to access your data

jwt_for_apis.what_is_jwt: JSON Web Token - a token format that contains user information

jwt_structure.signature: Server signs the token to prevent tampering

jwt_for_apis.jwt_format: Token has three parts separated by dots: header.payload.signature
jwt_advantages: Self-contained - token includes all needed info
Stateless - server doesn't need to look up token in database
Language-agnostic - can be used in any programming language

jwt_security.solution: Don't put sensitive data in token. Use HTTPS so token can't be intercepted.

jwt_security.concern: Token can't be revoked before expiration
jwt_security.solution: Use short expiration (15 min) plus refresh tokens for long sessions

jwt_security.concern: If secret key is leaked, all tokens are compromised
jwt_security.solution: Store secret key securely. Rotate keys regularly.

api_key_authentication.what_it_is: Simple token that identifies the application (not user)
api_key_authentication.use_case: For server-to-server APIs, or applications that don't have user login
api_key_authentication.security: API key is like a password - keep it secret. Can be rotated and revoked.

api_security_best_practices.why: All API traffic must be encrypted
Prevent injection attacks even in APIs
Prevent brute force, DDoS, and scraping
OAuth, JWT, or secure tokens. Not basic authentication
Allow old clients to keep working while deprecating old endpoints
Control which websites can call your API from browsers
Only return data user needs. Don't expose internal IDs or unnecessary fields.

topics.topic_name: Secure Coding Practices - Error Handling and Logging
topics.explanation: How developers write code affects security. Insecure coding practices create vulnerabilities even if all other security measures are in place.

error_handling.what_goes_wrong: Many developers expose too much information in error messages
error_handling.example_bad: Error: SQL error - SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=123. Table 'users' doesn't exist.
error_handling.problem: Attacker learns the database structure from error message
error_handling.example_good: An error occurred while processing your request. Please try again later or contact support.
error_handling.principle: Users see friendly message, developers see detailed logs

error_handling_best_practices.practice: Never Show Database Errors to Users
error_handling_best_practices.bad: SQL Error: Column 'password' does not exist
error_handling_best_practices.good: Unable to process your request. Error code: ERR001

error_handling_best_practices.practice: Never Show Stack Traces in Production
error_handling_best_practices.bad: Error at line 42 in application code, function getUserById()
error_handling_best_practices.good: An unexpected error occurred. Please contact support.

error_handling_best_practices.what_to_do: Write full error details to secure server logs, not to user
error_handling_best_practices.example: File stored securely on server (only accessible to developers)

error_handling_best_practices.why: Don't reveal whether username exists, whether email is registered, etc.
error_handling_best_practices.good: This email cannot be used for registration

error_handling_best_practices.what_it_means: Use try-catch blocks to prevent unhandled exceptions from crashing app or exposing info
error_handling_best_practices.example: Try to process payment. If error, catch it and show generic message.

what_to_log.log: Successful login, failed login (username, timestamp, IP), password change
Access denied, permission grant/revoke, role change
Malicious input detected, XSS attempt blocked, SQL injection attempt
Data access, data modification (who, what, when)
Admin login, config change, user created/deleted

what_not_to_log.why: Never log passwords. Not even hashed passwords.
Violates PCI compliance. Can lead to fines.
If log is leaked, attackers get API keys

what_not_to_log.sensitive_data: Full Email Addresses in logs accessible to all
what_not_to_log.why: Can be used for targeted phishing

logging_security.what_it_means: Logs should be written to a secure server, not local files
Only developers and security team can read logs
Logs cannot be modified or deleted (even by attacker who gains access)
Automatically alert if suspicious patterns appear in logs (100 failed logins from same IP, etc.)

logging_security.what_to_include: When event happened, who did it, from which IP, what result

code_review_and_testing.what_it_is: Another developer reviews code before merging
code_review_and_testing.catches: Security flaws, injection vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets

code_review_and_testing.what_it_is: Automated tools scan source code for vulnerabilities
Automated tools test running application for vulnerabilities
Security experts attempt to hack the application to find vulnerabilities
code_review_and_testing.frequency: At least annually before major releases

topics.topic_name: Practical Activity - Test Vulnerable Web Apps, Identify Flaws, Fix Code
topics.explanation: Now let's apply web security concepts by working with vulnerable applications and fixing security issues.

activity_1.task_name: Task 1: SQL Injection Vulnerability - Identify and Fix
activity_1.objective: Understand SQL injection by finding it in vulnerable code and writing secure code

vulnerable_code.code:
username = request.form['username']
password = request.form['password']
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='" + username + "' AND password='" + password + "'"
result = db.execute(query)
vulnerable_code.vulnerability: Username and password are directly concatenated into SQL. Attacker can enter: ' OR '1'='1' to bypass login.

vulnerability_analysis.analysis: Query is built by concatenating user input directly into SQL string

vulnerability_analysis.result: SQL becomes string that bypasses password check. The '1'='1' is always true.

vulnerability_analysis.impact: Attacker can log in as any user without knowing password. Full account compromise.

secure_code_solution.code:
username = request.form['username']
password = request.form['password']
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=? AND password=?"
result = db.execute(query, (username, password))
secure_code_solution.why_it_works: Database treats username and password as pure data, not as SQL code. Even if they contain SQL keywords, they're harmless strings.

alternative_solutions.note: Server-side procedures that accept parameters safely

testing_the_fix.test: Try injection again: Username: ' OR '1'='1'-- Password: anything
testing_the_fix.result: Login fails. The string is treated as a literal username, not SQL code.
Login succeeds if credentials are correct

activity_2.task_name: Task 2: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) - Identify and Fix
activity_2.objective: Find XSS vulnerabilities and implement proper output encoding

vulnerable_code.vulnerability: innerHTML is used with unsanitized user input. If comment.text contains JavaScript, it will be executed.

vulnerability_analysis.analysis: innerHTML interprets HTML and executes any JavaScript inside it

vulnerability_analysis.when_displayed: Image fails to load, onerror event fires, JavaScript executes, attacker receives session cookie

vulnerability_analysis.impact: Attacker steals session cookies of all users who view the comment. Can hijack their accounts.

secure_code_solution.fix: Use textContent instead of innerHTML (or use a library to escape HTML)
secure_code_solution.why_it_works: textContent treats content as plain text, not HTML. HTML tags are displayed as text, not interpreted.

alternative_solutions.when: Before sending comment to client, escape HTML characters

alternative_solutions.solution: Use a template framework with auto-escaping

alternative_solutions.effect: Browser refuses to execute inline scripts or scripts from external sources

testing_the_fix.result: Text is displayed as plain text, not executed. No alert appears.
Image tag is displayed as text, not interpreted. No alert appears.

activity_3.task_name: Task 3: Weak Authentication - Identify and Fix
activity_3.objective: Find weak authentication and implement proper security measures

vulnerabilities.risk: Attacker can try unlimited password combinations
Error message reveals if username exists
If password is stolen, account is fully compromised

improvements.code:
import bcrypt
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())
user = db.query(User).filter(User.username == username).first()
if user and bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), user.password):
  ...
return 'Invalid username or password' (don't say which is wrong)

failed_attempts = get_failed_attempts(username)
if failed_attempts >= 5:
  return 'Account locked. Try again in 30 minutes'
increase_failed_attempts(username)

pseudocode: 1. Check rate limiting: Has user tried login >5 times in 1 minute?
3. If user not found, still hash the password (prevents timing attacks) and return generic error
4. Compare password hash with stored hash
5. If match, increment login success counter and check if MFA is enabled
6. If MFA enabled, generate and send code
7. If user provides correct MFA code, create session and return success
8. Log all events for audit trail

activity_4.objective: Use automated tools to find web vulnerabilities
activity_4.what_is_zap: OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) is a free tool that automatically scans web applications for security vulnerabilities

installation.source: Download from the official OWASP security tools website
installation.file: Available for Windows, macOS, and Linux

installation.instruction: Open OWASP ZAP from Applications menu

scanning_a_website.instruction: File menu > New > Create a new session

scanning_a_website.example: Enter a vulnerable practice website URL for testing

scanning_a_website.instruction: Click 'Scan' button or access from Tools menu

scanning_a_website.what_appears: ZAP finds vulnerabilities and categorizes them by severity (High, Medium, Low, Informational)

understanding_scan_results.examples: Insecure cookies, missing security headers, path traversal

for_each_vulnerability_zap_shows.example: The application is vulnerable to SQL injection attacks
The specific endpoint where vulnerability was found
Shows the actual HTTP request and response
Use parameterized queries instead of string concatenation

activity_5.task_name: Task 5: Input Validation - Identify and Fix
activity_5.objective: Find missing input validation and implement whitelist validation

vulnerable_code.code:
username = request.form['username']
email = request.form['email']
age = request.form['age']
user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == current_user.id).first()
user.username = username
user.email = email
user.age = age
db.commit()

problems.attack: Email: not properly formatted or contains malicious code
Age: -5 or 999 or 'abc' (not a valid age)
Username: million character string causes database issues

step1_define_whitelist: Email: valid email format (use regex or library)

validation_testing.test: SQL injection: username=''; DROP TABLE users; --'

units.title: Unit 6: Access Control and Identity Management
units.description: Understand who gets access to what and how to verify their identity

modules.title: Access Control and Identity Management
modules.description: Understand who gets access to what and how to verify their identity

topics.topic_name: Authentication Methods - Passwords, Biometrics, Hardware Tokens
topics.explanation: Authentication is proving you are who you claim to be. There are many methods, each with different security levels and trade-offs.

authentication_methods_overview.common_principle: Something you know, something you have, or something you are

methods.description: Secret text string only you know
methods.strong_example: K7#mPq$9xW2@nL4vB - 16 characters, mixed case, numbers, symbols
vulnerabilities: Users write passwords on sticky notes
methods.best_practice: Passwords should be 12+ characters, complex, and unique per site

methods.use_case: ATM cards, phone unlock (4-6 digits), bank transfers
methods.strength: Lower than passwords - only numeric, fewer combinations
methods.vulnerability: Only 10,000 combinations for 4-digit PIN. Can be brute-forced in seconds.
methods.improvement: Use 6-8 digit PINs, implement lockout after failed attempts

methods.description: Pre-defined questions you answer (e.g., 'What is your mother's maiden name?')
methods.problem: Answers can be guessed or researched (maiden names are public records)
methods.vulnerability: Social engineering - attacker calls company pretending to be you
methods.limitation: Should never be sole authentication method

methods.description: Longer phrase instead of single word (e.g., 'MyDogAte3GreenApples!OnTuesday')
methods.advantage: Easier to remember than random password, but still secure
methods.benefit: Length compensates for using actual words

methods.description: Physical device that generates codes or stores credentials
examples: YubiKey - USB device, small and portable
RSA SecurID - Generates new 6-digit code every 30 seconds
Smart card - Contains a chip with digital certificate
methods.how_it_works: Token generates one-time code or responds to server challenge
methods.strength: Very high - physical device required, can't be duplicated remotely
methods.disadvantage: Must carry the device, can be lost or stolen

methods.description: Credit-card-sized device with embedded microchip containing certificate
methods.how_it_works: Card stores private key. Computer reads card and uses key for authentication.
methods.disadvantage: Requires card reader, can be lost

methods.description: Receive code via text message or generated by authenticator app
methods.sms_method: Server sends code to your phone via SMS
methods.app_method: Authenticator app generates code (Google Authenticator, Authy)
methods.strength_sms: Medium - SMS can be intercepted or SIM swapped
methods.strength_app: High - code generated locally on device, not transmitted
methods.common_use: Two-factor authentication for email, banking, social media

methods.description: Server sends notification to your phone. You tap 'Approve' to confirm login.
methods.how_it_works: User tries to log in, phone gets push notification, user taps Approve
methods.advantage: User-friendly, no need to type codes
methods.strength: High - attacker must have physical access to phone
methods.example: Microsoft Authenticator, Google Authenticator push notifications

methods.description: Single-use code valid for short period (usually 30 seconds)
methods.strength: High - code expires quickly, can't be reused
methods.limitation: Must enter code within time window

methods.how_it_works: Device captures fingerprint, stores pattern, compares future scans
methods.strength: High - fingerprint unique to each person, difficult to spoof
methods.vulnerability: Fingerprints can be lifted from surfaces and used to create fake fingerprints
methods.spoofing: Advanced attackers can create fake fingerprints with clay or silicone
methods.use_case: Phone unlock, access to sensitive areas, banking
methods.disadvantage: Can't be changed if compromised (unlike password)

methods.how_it_works: Device captures face, creates facial template, compares with stored template
methods.modern_systems: Can detect and prevent spoofing with liveness detection (detecting if live person or photo)
methods.strength: High - difficult to spoof, especially with liveness detection
methods.vulnerability: Early systems fooled by photos. Modern systems require liveness.
methods.spoofing_prevention: Requires blink, head movement, or other live indicators
methods.use_case: Phone unlock (iPhone Face ID), border control, banking apps
methods.privacy_concern: Captured biometric data could be used for surveillance
methods.accuracy: Works well in good lighting, can fail with glasses or beard

methods.description: Scan of iris (colored part) or blood vessels in retina
methods.accuracy: Very high - iris patterns are highly unique
methods.strength: Extremely high - nearly impossible to spoof or forge
methods.disadvantage: Requires specialized hardware (not common on consumer devices)
methods.privacy: Iris recognition doesn't require consent like face recognition

methods.how_it_works: Capture voice sample, create voice print, compare with stored print
methods.vulnerability: Can be spoofed with recordings or speech synthesis
methods.liveness_detection: Ask user to speak specific phrase or passphrases
methods.accuracy: Affected by background noise, voice changes due to illness

methods.description: Analyze how you interact (typing speed, mouse movement, walking pattern)
methods.keystroke_dynamics: How fast you type, time between keystrokes
methods.mouse_movement: Pattern of mouse movements, clicking speed
methods.gait_recognition: How you walk (stride length, speed, arm movement)
methods.strength: Passive - works in background without user action
methods.limitation: Can change over time or vary with circumstances
methods.use_case: Fraud detection, continuous authentication in banking

multi_factor_authentication_mfa.what_it_is: Combining two or more authentication methods
examples: Password (something you know) + SMS code (something you have)
Hardware token (something you have) + PIN (something you know)
multi_factor_authentication_mfa.why_it_matters: If attacker steals one factor, they still can't access account without other factors
multi_factor_authentication_mfa.real_world_example: Bank login: Enter username and password, then confirm with fingerprint on phone
multi_factor_authentication_mfa.security_increase: MFA reduces account compromise risk by 99%

topics.topic_name: Authorization Models - RBAC and ABAC
topics.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user can do. There are two main models: Role-Based (RBAC) and Attribute-Based (ABAC).

authorization_definition.what_it_is: Deciding what resources a user can access and what actions they can perform
authorization_definition.vs_authentication: Authentication: Who are you? Authorization: What are you allowed to do?
authorization_definition.principle: Principle of Least Privilege - users get minimum permissions needed

rbac_role_based_access_control.what_it_is: Users are assigned roles, and roles have permissions
flow: Role has specific permissions (e.g., 'Can create reports', 'Can approve timesheets')
When user tries to do action, system checks: Does user's role have this permission?
If yes, action is allowed. If no, action is denied.

simple_example.organization: A company with employees, managers, and admins

advantages: Easy to manage - assign roles instead of individual permissions
disadvantages: Rigid - doesn't account for context or conditions
Role explosion - too many roles needed for complex requirements
All users in same role get same permissions (no exceptions)

roles: User - Can post, comment, like, message friends
Moderator - Can post, comment, delete inappropriate content
Admin - All permissions plus manage users and settings

abac_attribute_based_access_control.what_it_is: Access decisions based on attributes (characteristics) of users, resources, and environment

how_it_works.rule_example: Allow access IF (user.department == 'Finance' AND resource.classification == 'public' AND time_of_day >= 9:00 AND time_of_day <= 17:00)
how_it_works.evaluation: System evaluates all conditions before granting access

rules.rule: Allow access IF (user.role == 'Doctor' AND resource.is_my_patient == true AND user.department == 'Cardiology') THEN Read, Write
rules.means: Doctor can read/write records only for their own patients in their department

rules.rule: Allow access IF (user.role == 'Nurse' AND resource.is_my_ward == true) THEN Read
rules.means: Nurse can read records for patients in their ward only

rules.rule: Allow access IF (user.role == 'Admin' AND user.location == 'Head Office') THEN All permissions
rules.means: Admin can do everything only when at head office

advantages: Context-aware - considers time, location, and other conditions
Flexible - adapt to complex requirements without creating new roles
Dynamic - rules can change without changing user roles
disadvantages: Performance overhead - more conditions to evaluate
Difficult to understand for non-technical people

rules: Allow edit if user is file owner
Allow view if user is in shared group AND current_time < expiration_time
Allow download if user.location == 'company_network' OR user.ip_address in whitelist
Deny all if user.account_suspicious == true OR failed_login_attempts > 5

comparison.abac: Requires policy engine and attribute management

acl_access_control_lists.what_it_is: For each resource, specify who can access it and what they can do
acl_access_control_lists.format: File ABC: Owner (read, write, delete), Group X (read), Public (none)
acl_access_control_lists.use_case: File systems, cloud storage, document sharing
acl_access_control_lists.example: Windows NTFS file permissions - right-click file, Properties, Security tab shows ACL

topics.topic_name: Directory Services - Active Directory and LDAP
topics.explanation: Directory services store and manage information about users, groups, computers, and other network resources. They centralize identity management.

what_are_directory_services.definition: Centralized database of information about network users and resources
what_are_directory_services.purpose: Single place to manage who can access what on the network
what_are_directory_services.analogy: Like a phone directory that not only has phone numbers, but also permissions and properties

ldap_lightweight_directory_access_protoc.what_it_is: Protocol (set of rules) for accessing directory services
ldap_lightweight_directory_access_protoc.ldap_as_standard: LDAP is the industry standard for directory access
ldap_lightweight_directory_access_protoc.not_a_directory: LDAP is not a directory itself - it's how you access a directory
how_it_works: Client connects to LDAP server (usually port 389 for unencrypted, 636 for encrypted)
Client sends LDAP query (e.g., 'Find user with username=john')
Server searches directory database and returns results
Client receives information about the user

ldap_structure.hierarchy: LDAP organizes information in a tree structure (like file folders)

components.example: cn=john represents specific user named John

ldap_attributes.what_stored: LDAP stores attributes about each object
examples: username, password hash, email, phone, department
employee ID, manager, office location, job title

ldap_bind.process: Client provides username and password, LDAP server validates
ldap_bind.use_case: Logging into network resources using LDAP credentials

active_directory.what_it_is: Microsoft's directory service built on LDAP
active_directory.relationship_to_ldap: Active Directory is an implementation of LDAP with additional features
additional_features: Group Policy - Apply settings to users and computers automatically
Trust relationships - Multiple domains can trust each other
how_it_works: Administrator creates user account in Active Directory
User logs into their Windows computer using AD credentials
Computer contacts Domain Controller (Active Directory server)
Domain Controller verifies credentials using Kerberos protocol
User is granted access with appropriate permissions

active_directory_structure.domain: Collection of users and computers (e.g., sales.company.com)
active_directory_structure.group: Collection of users with common permissions

group_policy.what_it_is: Centralized way to apply settings to users and computers
examples: Require password minimum length of 12 characters
Set screensaver to activate after 15 minutes of inactivity
Force Windows updates on specific schedule
Deploy software to all computers in a department
group_policy.benefit: Single setting applies to all users/computers without manually configuring each one

directory_service_benefits.example: Add user once, they get access to all systems using that directory
Same permissions applied across all connected systems
Easy to manage thousands of users from one place
New hire gets access to all needed systems immediately
Disable one account, user loses access to everything

directory_service_security.security_concern: Directory serves as single point of failure
directory_service_security.mitigation: Use multiple domain controllers for redundancy

directory_service_security.security_concern: If directory is compromised, attacker has access to all credentials
directory_service_security.mitigation: Secure domain controllers, require strong admin passwords, enable logging

directory_service_security.security_concern: LDAP credentials sent over network in plaintext
directory_service_security.mitigation: Use LDAPS (LDAP over SSL/TLS) to encrypt traffic
Enforce strong password policy through Group Policy

topics.topic_name: Single Sign-On (SSO) - Centralized Authentication
topics.explanation: SSO allows users to log in once and gain access to multiple systems without re-entering credentials. Improves security and user experience.

what_is_sso.definition: User authenticates once and gains access to multiple systems
what_is_sso.benefit: Users don't need to remember multiple passwords
what_is_sso.security_benefit: Centralized authentication makes security easier to manage

workflow: User logs into email with username and password
User logs into project management tool with different username and password
User logs into file sharing system with another username and password
User logs into CRM with yet another set of credentials
User has 4 different passwords to manage
User logs into SSO portal with username and password
User is now authenticated across all systems
User can access email, project tool, file sharing, and CRM without additional login
User only needs to remember one password

basic_process: Application A redirects user to SSO server (e.g., Okta, Azure AD)
User logs in to SSO server with credentials
SSO server validates credentials and issues a token/session
User is redirected back to application A with token
Application A receives token and allows access
Application B redirects to SSO server
SSO server recognizes user (already logged in) and immediately issues token
User gains access to application B without entering password again

sso_protocols.what_it_is: XML-based format for exchanging authentication information
sso_protocols.how_it_works: SSO provider sends XML assertion about user identity to application
sso_protocols.use: Enterprise systems, commonly in corporate environments
sso_protocols.example: User logs in via corporate SSO, gets SAML assertion, accesses company applications

sso_protocols.what_it_is: Protocol for delegated access without sharing passwords
sso_protocols.how_it_works: User authorizes application to access their info from SSO provider
sso_protocols.use: Third-party applications, mobile apps, modern web apps
sso_protocols.example: Log in with Google, Facebook, or Microsoft account

sso_protocols.what_it_is: Layer on top of OAuth 2.0 for authentication
sso_protocols.advantage: Combines security of SAML with simplicity of OAuth

sso_protocols.how_it_works: Tickets are used instead of passing passwords repeatedly

sso_benefits.description: Users only log in once instead of multiple times
Users remember one strong password instead of many weak ones
Centralized authentication, easier to enforce strong policies
New employees get access to all systems through single SSO
Disable SSO account, employee loses access to everything
All logins recorded in one place

sso_risks.description: If SSO server is down, no one can log in
Attacker has access to all systems
sso_risks.mitigation: Require MFA at SSO, monitor unusual access patterns

sso_risks.description: Once logged in, user has access to many systems for extended period
sso_risks.mitigation: Require re-authentication for sensitive operations, session timeout

sso_risks.description: If user forgets to log out, next person has access to all their systems
sso_risks.mitigation: Educate users, auto-logout, require re-auth for sensitive operations

sso_implementation_requirements: Centralized identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Keycloak, etc.)
Applications must support SSO protocol (SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect)
Secure communication between applications and SSO provider
User attributes synced from directory service
Policies for session duration and re-authentication

topics.topic_name: Privilege Escalation - How Attackers Exploit It, How to Prevent It
topics.explanation: Privilege escalation is when an attacker gains higher-level permissions than they initially have. Understanding and preventing it is critical.

what_is_privilege_escalation.definition: Gaining access to higher privilege level than you're authorized for
examples: Limited user executes system commands that only admins can run

vertical_privilege_escalation.what_it_is: User gains permissions above their assigned role
vertical_privilege_escalation.attack_vector: Find vulnerability in system to bypass authorization checks
how_it_happens: System has bug where authorization not properly checked
System doesn't verify user is admin, allows access
User is now functioning as admin

real_example.vulnerability: Website stores user role in browser localStorage
real_example.how_attacked: User opens browser console, changes localStorage.role = 'admin'
real_example.result: Website now treats user as admin

prevention: Always verify authorization on server-side, never trust client-side role
Check permissions before every privileged operation
Use whitelist of allowed permissions, not blacklist of denied
Log all attempts to access resources above user's privilege level

horizontal_privilege_escalation.what_it_is: User gains access to another user's resources at same privilege level
horizontal_privilege_escalation.example: User A accesses User B's private data (both are regular users)
horizontal_privilege_escalation.attack_vector: Access resources by changing ID in URL or request
how_it_happens: User A views their profile at /user/profile/123
System doesn't verify User A owns profile 456

real_example.attack: User changes recipient_id to 'admin_user' or high-value account
real_example.result: Transfer goes to attacker's chosen account

prevention: Always verify user owns the resource before returning it
Use indirect references instead of direct IDs when possible
Validate that user has permission to access specific record
Use database queries that filter by current user: SELECT * FROM data WHERE owner_id = current_user_id

privilege_escalation_techniques.example: Zero-day vulnerability in OS kernel allows privilege escalation
privilege_escalation_techniques.real_case: Windows privilege escalation bug let user run code as System account

privilege_escalation_techniques.example: Sensitive config file is readable by all users
privilege_escalation_techniques.attack: Regular user reads config file, finds admin password
privilege_escalation_techniques.prevention: Set proper file permissions (chmod 600 for sensitive files)

privilege_escalation_techniques.example: sudo configured to allow user to run any command as root without password
privilege_escalation_techniques.sudoers_file: User can run 'sudo su' without password, becomes root
privilege_escalation_techniques.prevention: Restrict sudo to necessary commands only, require password

privilege_escalation_techniques.example: Program with SUID bit can run with owner's permissions
privilege_escalation_techniques.attack: Vulnerable program runs as root, attacker exploits vulnerability
privilege_escalation_techniques.prevention: Only use SUID when necessary, audit SUID binaries

privilege_escalation_techniques.how: Attacker places malicious DLL where program looks for libraries
privilege_escalation_techniques.result: Program loads malicious code with its permissions
privilege_escalation_techniques.prevention: Use full paths to libraries, validate library signatures

privilege_escalation_techniques.example: Web app checks permission in JavaScript on client-side
privilege_escalation_techniques.attack: Attacker disables JavaScript check or modifies request

privilege_escalation_in_different_system.common_exploits: UAC bypass, kernel vulnerabilities, weak file permissions
SUID binaries, sudo misconfiguration, kernel vulnerabilities
Authorization bypass, insecure direct object reference, broken access control

preventing_privilege_escalation.example: Web server runs as 'www-data' user, not root

preventing_privilege_escalation.where: Check on server-side, every single time, don't trust client

preventing_privilege_escalation.good: Permissions stored on server, checked server-side

preventing_privilege_escalation.how: Only allow specific commands, require password

preventing_privilege_escalation.what_to_log: Failed authorization, attempts to access resources

topics.topic_name: Audit Logging - Tracking Who Did What and When
topics.explanation: Audit logs record security-relevant events. They're essential for detecting attacks, investigating incidents, and demonstrating compliance.

what_is_audit_logging.definition: Recording security-relevant events with enough detail to reconstruct what happened

why_audit_logs_matter.example: Notice 1000 failed logins from same IP in 1 hour = brute force attack
Data breach discovered. Review logs to see who accessed what data and when.
Auditor asks: Who accessed customer data? Show audit log.
Employee deletes customer record. Audit log shows who did it and when.
After incident, recreate exact sequence of events from logs

log: Failed login (user, timestamp, source IP, reason)
Role assignment (user, role, timestamp, who assigned)
Database query (user, query, timestamp, affected records)
Configuration change (admin, setting, old_value, new_value, timestamp)
Malicious input detected (type, user, timestamp, input)
XSS attempt blocked (user, timestamp, payload snippet)
SQL injection attempt (user, timestamp, suspicious query)
Privilege escalation attempt (user, timestamp, what was attempted)

what_not_to_log.why: Never log passwords, not even hashed
PCI DSS compliance violation, security risk
If log is compromised, so are the secrets
If logged, could be stolen from logs

what_to_include: Action (what was done: login, delete, modify, read)
Resource (what was affected: file, record, system)
log_details.example_good_log: 2024-03-15 14:23:45.123 UTC | user=john | action=file_delete | resource=/reports/sales_2024.pdf | result=success | source_ip=192.168.1.100 | source_app=DocumentManager

log_security.security_concern: Logs can be altered or deleted by attacker to cover tracks
log_security.solution: Make logs immutable - cannot be modified or deleted after creation

log_security.security_concern: Logs contain sensitive information and could be breached
log_security.solution: Encrypt logs at rest. Restrict access to authorized personnel only.

log_security.security_concern: Logs stored on same server as application
log_security.solution: Send logs to separate secure log server for redundancy
Use SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) to analyze logs

log_retention.how_long: Depends on compliance requirements and use cases
log_retention.archive: Old logs should be archived to cheaper storage but kept immutable

log_analysis_and_monitoring.example: Alert if failed login attempts exceed 5 in 5 minutes from same IP
Detect unusual access patterns (accessing resources user never accesses before)
Correlate failed logins from same IP with data downloads - possible attack
Establish normal user behavior, alert on deviations

siem_security_information_event_manageme.what_it_is: System that collects, correlates, and analyzes logs from multiple sources
siem_security_information_event_manageme.purpose: Make sense of massive amounts of log data
siem_security_information_event_manageme.examples: Splunk, ELK Stack, IBM QRadar, ArcSight

events: 2:00 PM - Failed login attempt for user 'admin' from IP 203.0.113.50
2:05 PM - Failed login attempt for user 'admin' from same IP (attempt 2)
2:10 PM - Failed login attempt for user 'admin' from same IP (attempt 3)
2:15 PM - Failed login attempt for user 'admin' from same IP (attempt 4)
2:20 PM - Failed login attempt for user 'admin' from same IP (attempt 5)
2:20 PM - System ALERT: Brute force attack detected. Account 'admin' locked for 30 minutes.
2:21 PM - ALERT sent to security team
2:30 PM - Security team investigates IP 203.0.113.50, identifies as VPN from foreign country
2:35 PM - Security team contacts admin user, confirms didn't attempt login
2:36 PM - IP 203.0.113.50 added to block list
2:40 PM - Admin account is unlocked after 30-minute lockout
practical_example.what_logs_enabled: Detection of brute force attack in progress, quick response time, prevention of account compromise

topics.topic_name: Practical Activity - Access Control Implementation and Testing
topics.explanation: Apply access control concepts by implementing authorization, testing permissions, and reviewing audit logs.

activity_1.task_name: Task 1: Implement RBAC in a Simple Application
activity_1.objective: Understand role-based access control by implementing roles and permissions
activity_1.scenario: Building a simple blog platform with different user roles

implementation_steps.sql: CREATE TABLE roles (id INTEGER, name VARCHAR(50), description VARCHAR(255))
CREATE TABLE role_permissions (role_id INTEGER, permission VARCHAR(50))
CREATE TABLE user_roles (user_id INTEGER, role_id INTEGER)
INSERT INTO roles VALUES (1, 'User', 'Basic user role'), (2, 'Editor', 'Editor role'), (3, 'Admin', 'Administrator role')

implementation_steps.code: For User role: INSERT INTO role_permissions VALUES (1, 'view_published_posts'), (1, 'create_own_posts'), etc.

testing_the_implementation.test: Regular user tries to delete another user's post
testing_the_implementation.expected: Denied - user doesn't have delete_all_posts permission

testing_the_implementation.test: Editor tries to delete a post
testing_the_implementation.expected: Denied - editor can only delete own posts (unless they wrote it)

testing_the_implementation.test: Admin tries to delete any post
User tries to publish a post
testing_the_implementation.expected: Denied - users can't publish, only editors and admins

activity_2.task_name: Task 2: Test for Broken Access Control Vulnerabilities
activity_2.objective: Find authorization bugs by attempting to access resources you shouldn't have access to

vulnerability_1.name: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
vulnerability_1.test: Change ID to /user/profile?id=456 and see if you can view another user's profile
vulnerability_1.vulnerable_if: You can see another user's private information without being admin
vulnerability_1.fix: Always verify user owns the profile: if (user_id != requested_id) { deny_access }

vulnerability_2.name: Missing Authorization Check
vulnerability_2.test: As regular user, try to access /admin/users directly
vulnerability_2.vulnerable_if: You can access admin page and see all users without being admin
vulnerability_2.fix: Check if user is admin before loading admin page: if (!is_admin) { redirect_to_home }

vulnerability_3.name: Client-Side Permission Check
vulnerability_3.scenario: Delete button only shows for own posts
vulnerability_3.test: Open browser developer tools, find the delete button code, enable it for other user's posts
vulnerability_3.vulnerable_if: You can delete other user's posts by enabling hidden button
vulnerability_3.fix: Always verify server-side: if (post_owner == user_id) { allow_delete }

vulnerability_4.name: Parameter Tampering
vulnerability_4.scenario: Transfer funds form with hidden field: recipient_id=789
vulnerability_4.test: Modify recipient_id to your own account using browser console
vulnerability_4.vulnerable_if: Transfer goes to your account instead of intended recipient
vulnerability_4.fix: Verify recipient_id on server-side, don't trust client-side values

testing_checklist: Try to access resources you shouldn't have access to
Try to modify IDs in URLs to access other users' data
Try to enable hidden buttons or modify JavaScript
Try to change user role in browser storage
Try to access admin functions as regular user
Try to perform actions you shouldn't be allowed to do

activity_3.task_name: Task 3: Review and Analyze Audit Logs
activity_3.objective: Understand how to interpret audit logs and detect suspicious activity

analysis_questions.question: What is normal activity for user Alice?
analysis_questions.answer: Login from 192.168.1.100 during business hours, viewing and editing documents, logout at end of day

analysis_questions.question: What is suspicious about the second set of logs?
analysis_questions.answer: 5 failed login attempts in 15 seconds from different IP (203.0.113.50), outside business hours. This is a brute force attack.

analysis_questions.question: What happened in response?
analysis_questions.answer: System automatically locked the account after 5 failed attempts, preventing further attacks

analysis_questions.question: What should happen next?
analysis_questions.answer: Security team should investigate the IP, contact user Alice to confirm she didn't attempt login, review what happened before account was locked

red_flags_in_logs: Multiple failed logins in short time
Login from unusual IP or location
Access to resources outside normal work hours
Access to sensitive resources by non-admin user
Deletion of records by unauthorized user
Unusual access patterns compared to baseline

activity_4.task_name: Task 4: Detect and Prevent Privilege Escalation
activity_4.objective: Find privilege escalation vulnerabilities and implement fixes

vulnerable_code.vulnerability: Authorization check is weak - doesn't verify on critical operations

attack_scenario: Attacker finds user ID 1 (admin) in URL: /admin/users/1
Authorization check only verifies role in JavaScript
Attacker opens browser console and modifies role variable to 'admin'
Admin is deleted - privilege escalation successful

improvements: Always verify authorization on server-side, never trust client
Check authorization for EVERY action, not just some
Use database to verify user role, not client-side variable

testing_the_fix.test: Regular user tries to delete another user
Admin deletes user from API directly
testing_the_fix.result: Allowed, action logged in audit trail

testing_the_fix.test: Attacker modifies client-side role variable to 'admin'
testing_the_fix.result: Doesn't work - server verifies role from database, not client
All privilege escalation attempts are recorded

activity_5.task_name: Task 5: Set Up Audit Logging System
activity_5.objective: Implement comprehensive audit logging to track all security-relevant events

log_structure.example: 2024-03-15 14:23:45.123 UTC | user_id=42 | action=file_delete | resource=/documents/confidential.pdf | result=success | source_ip=192.168.1.100 | status_code=200

implementation.sql: CREATE TABLE audit_logs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, timestamp DATETIME, user_id INTEGER, action VARCHAR(50), resource VARCHAR(255), result VARCHAR(20), source_ip VARCHAR(15))

implementation.policy: Keep logs for minimum 1 year, archive older logs

implementation.alert: Alert if failed login attempts > 5 in 5 minutes from same IP

what_to_log: All authentication events (login, logout, failed login)
All administrative actions (user creation, deletion, role changes)
All security events (malicious input, attacks blocked)
All system changes (config changes, software updates)

log_analysis_exercise.scenario: Review these logs and identify the attack
log_analysis_exercise.analysis: User 22 downloaded 3 sensitive files in 20 minutes. Normal behavior is to access files occasionally for work. This could indicate data theft or competitive espionage. Should investigate what user does and if downloads are justified.
