modules.title: Threat Analysis and Risk Management
modules.description: Learn how to identify, assess, and prioritize security risks

topics.topic_name: Threat Modeling - STRIDE Methodology and Attack Trees
topics.explanation: Threat modeling is systematically identifying potential threats to a system before they become problems. It helps you think like an attacker.

what_is_threat_modeling.definition: Process of identifying potential threats to a system and how attackers might exploit it
what_is_threat_modeling.purpose: Find vulnerabilities early in design phase, before systems are built and deployed
what_is_threat_modeling.benefit: Fixing vulnerabilities in design is cheaper than fixing after breach

threat_modeling_process.step1: Define the system - What are we protecting? What are the boundaries?
threat_modeling_process.step2: Create data flow diagram - Show how data moves through the system
threat_modeling_process.step3: Identify threats - What could go wrong? Who might attack us?
threat_modeling_process.step4: Rank threats - Which are most dangerous? Which are most likely?
threat_modeling_process.step5: Mitigate threats - What can we do to prevent or reduce risk?
threat_modeling_process.step6: Validate - Did our mitigations work? Are we now secure?

stride_methodology.what_is_stride: Framework for identifying security threats using six categories
stride_methodology.acronym: STRIDE = Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege

categories.definition: Attacker pretends to be someone else
categories.example: Attacker sends email pretending to be CEO, asking employee to transfer funds
categories.technical_example: Attacker spoofs IP address to bypass IP-based access control
categories.real_world: Phishing emails claiming to be from your bank
categories.mitigation: Multi-factor authentication, digital signatures, strong authentication

categories.definition: Attacker modifies data or code without authorization
categories.example: Attacker intercepts network packet and changes amount from $100 to $1000
categories.technical_example: Modifying HTML in browser to change price before submitting form
categories.real_world: Man-in-the-middle attack modifying wire transfer amount
categories.mitigation: Use HTTPS/TLS, data validation, integrity checks, digital signatures

categories.definition: Attacker denies they did something, or claims they didn't
categories.example: User claims they didn't send an email or approve a transfer
categories.technical_example: No audit logs - can't prove who performed an action
categories.real_world: Employee denies deleting customer records, but no evidence exists
categories.mitigation: Audit logging, digital signatures, non-repudiation controls

categories.definition: Attacker gains access to information they shouldn't see
categories.example: Hacker views other users' medical records in health app
categories.technical_example: SQL injection reveals password hashes from database
categories.real_world: Accidental exposure of API keys on GitHub, found by attacker
categories.mitigation: Encryption, access control, data masking, secure disposal

categories.definition: Attacker prevents legitimate users from accessing service
categories.example: DDoS attack floods server with requests, making it unavailable
categories.technical_example: Sending so many SQL queries that database becomes unresponsive
categories.real_world: Competitor launches DDoS attack during Black Friday sales
categories.mitigation: Rate limiting, DDoS protection, redundancy, load balancing

categories.definition: User gains higher permissions than they should have
categories.example: Regular user becomes admin and deletes all data
categories.technical_example: SQL injection in login form bypasses authentication
categories.real_world: Employee discovers weak sudo configuration, runs commands as root
categories.mitigation: Proper authorization checks, least privilege, strong authentication

data_flows: Browser sends credentials to server via HTTPS
Browser uses token for subsequent requests

threats_identified.description: Attacker creates fake login page that looks like real bank
threats_identified.user_impact: User enters credentials into fake site, attacker gets password
threats_identified.mitigation: Use SSL certificates, display bank name prominently, educate users

threats_identified.description: Attacker intercepts network traffic and changes transfer amount
threats_identified.user_impact: Customer tries to send $100 but $10,000 is transferred
threats_identified.mitigation: Use HTTPS/TLS to encrypt all traffic, add digital signatures

threats_identified.description: Customer claims they didn't approve a $500 purchase
threats_identified.user_impact: Bank can't prove customer authorized the transaction
threats_identified.mitigation: Audit logging, SMS confirmation, transaction history display

threats_identified.description: Attacker accesses other customers' account balances through URL tampering
threats_identified.user_impact: Privacy violation, attacker sees financial information
threats_identified.mitigation: Verify user owns account before showing data, proper access control

threats_identified.description: Competitor launches DDoS during customer payroll processing
threats_identified.user_impact: Thousands of employees can't access accounts to view salary
threats_identified.mitigation: DDoS protection, redundant servers, rate limiting

threats_identified.description: Regular customer finds bug in admin panel, gains admin access
threats_identified.user_impact: Attacker can view all customer data, freeze accounts
threats_identified.mitigation: Proper authorization checks, security testing, principle of least privilege

attack_trees.what_it_is: Visual representation of how an attacker might compromise a system
attack_trees.format: Tree diagram with goal at top, attack methods as branches
attack_trees.use_case: Break down complex attacks into simpler steps

attack_tree_example.goal: Steal customer data from banking system

sub_attacks: Poison DNS to redirect to fake site
Pretend to be IT support, get password
Plant USB in parking lot with malware
Access server room and steal hard drives

attack_tree_example.probability_assessment: Each leaf has estimated probability of success
attack_tree_example.impact_assessment: If successful, how much damage could attacker do?

topics.topic_name: Vulnerability Assessment - Scanning, Classification, Severity Rating
topics.explanation: Vulnerability assessment is finding and measuring security weaknesses in systems. It's like a health checkup for security.

what_is_vulnerability_assessment.definition: Systematic process of identifying, classifying, and prioritizing security weaknesses
what_is_vulnerability_assessment.vs_threat_modeling: Threat modeling is designing defensively. Vulnerability assessment finds actual problems in deployed systems.
what_is_vulnerability_assessment.when_done: Before going to production, regularly after deployment, after updates, after incidents

vulnerability_scanning.what_it_is: Using automated tools to systematically search for known vulnerabilities

scan_types.scope: Entire network - all devices and systems
scan_types.finds: Unpatched systems, weak services, network misconfigurations
SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, broken authentication, weak encryption
Default passwords, unnecessary services, weak encryption settings

scan_types.scope: System compliance with standards (PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001)
scan_types.finds: Non-compliance with security standards and regulations

vulnerability_classification.what_it_is: Organizing vulnerabilities into categories for better understanding

classification_schemes.what_it_is: List of software weaknesses that can lead to vulnerabilities
classification_schemes.example: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS)

classification_schemes.what_it_is: Unique ID for each known vulnerability
classification_schemes.example: CVE-2021-44228: Log4Shell vulnerability in Java logging library

classification_schemes.what_it_is: List of top 10 web application security risks

by_type: Network vulnerabilities - Open ports, weak protocols
Application vulnerabilities - Code flaws, logic errors
Cryptographic vulnerabilities - Weak encryption, poor key management

severity_rating.what_it_is: Assigning importance level to each vulnerability
severity_rating.why_it_matters: Helps prioritize which vulnerabilities to fix first

cvss_common_vulnerability_scoring_system.what_it_is: Industry standard for rating vulnerability severity

severity_ratings.meaning: Significant impact, requires some effort to exploit
Maximum impact, trivial to exploit, likely already being exploited

vulnerability_example_with_scoring.description: User input not validated, attacker can execute arbitrary SQL

cvss_calculation.attack_vector: Network (3.9 points) - Can be exploited remotely
cvss_calculation.attack_complexity: Low (0 points) - No special conditions needed
cvss_calculation.privileges_required: None (3.1 points) - Attacker doesn't need account
cvss_calculation.user_interaction: None (3.2 points) - No user action required
cvss_calculation.impact_confidentiality: High (3.1 points) - All data can be read
cvss_calculation.impact_integrity: High (3.1 points) - All data can be modified
cvss_calculation.impact_availability: High (3.1 points) - Database can be deleted

vulnerability_example_with_scoring.interpretation: Extremely dangerous - can lead to complete database compromise. Fix immediately.

topics.topic_name: Risk Calculation - Likelihood × Impact
topics.explanation: Risk is not just about how likely something is. It's also about how bad the consequences would be. Risk = Likelihood × Impact.

risk_definition.meaning: A highly likely threat with minimal impact is different from unlikely threat with catastrophic impact

likelihood.what_it_is: How probable is this threat to actually happen?
likelihood.scale: 0 - 1 (0 = will never happen, 1 = will definitely happen)

examples.threat: Employee password written on sticky note
Nuclear power plant physically destroyed by weather
examples.reason: Rare occurrence, plants are built to withstand

examples.threat: Cloud storage provider suffers total data loss
examples.reason: Major providers have redundancy and backups

impact.what_it_is: If threat occurs, how bad are the consequences?

examples.reason: All encrypted data becomes readable, complete confidentiality breach
Network down for a few hours, annoying but not devastating

risk_matrix.concept: Plot threats on grid with likelihood on one axis, impact on other
risk_matrix.high_likelihood_low_impact: Fix soon - happens often but less serious
risk_matrix.low_likelihood_high_impact: Important to address - rare but catastrophic if happens
risk_matrix.low_likelihood_low_impact: Lowest priority - can be ignored or addressed eventually

threat_1.name: SQL Injection in Login Form
threat_1.likelihood: 0.9 (90%) - Very likely if not fixed, commonly exploited
threat_1.action: Fix immediately, this is top priority

threat_2.name: Employee Password Written on Sticky Note
threat_2.impact: 0.7 (70%) - Account compromise, but limited to that one person
threat_2.action: Implement password manager and security training

threat_3.name: Typo in System Configuration File
threat_3.action: Implement configuration validation and code review

acceptable_risk.what_it_is: Organization determines what level of risk they can tolerate
acceptable_risk.risk_threshold: Example: Accept risks below 0.1 (10%), mitigate risks 0.1-0.5, immediately fix risks above 0.5
factors_affecting: Industry (healthcare has lower tolerance than casual gaming)
Regulatory requirements (PCI DSS, HIPAA require low risk)
Business model (bank needs higher security than startup)

topics.topic_name: Incident Classification - Severity Levels
topics.explanation: When a security incident happens, you need to quickly classify it to determine how to respond. Severity determines urgency and resources needed.

incident_definition.what_it_is: Security event that violates security policy or causes harm

severity_levels.description: Immediate threat to business operations or data
severity_levels.team_involvement: All hands on deck - drop other work
examples: Active ransomware encryption of production servers
Attacker has live access to systems
Complete database breach with customer data exposure
severity_levels.response: Stop the incident NOW, prevent spread, contain damage

severity_levels.description: Significant security incident with potential for serious impact
examples: Confirmed unauthorized access to internal systems
Data exfiltration in progress (attacker downloading files)
severity_levels.response: Isolate affected systems, gather evidence, investigate cause

severity_levels.description: Security incident that requires attention but not immediate
examples: Suspicious login from unusual location (but user confirms)
Phishing email received by employee (but not clicked)
severity_levels.response: Investigate, determine if mitigation needed, monitor for escalation

severity_levels.description: Minor security issue, no urgent action needed
severity_levels.response_time: Within 24 hours or during next business hours
examples: Employee found with unencrypted USB drive
Policy violation with no actual impact
severity_levels.response: Document, schedule fix, implement preventive measures

consider: What data is affected? (public, internal, confidential, sensitive)
How many users are impacted? (1, 10, 1000, all)
Business impact - Can business operate? (no impact, partial impact, full outage)
Is attack ongoing? (just detected vs. active attack)
Can data be recovered? (yes, difficult, impossible)

incident_classification_example.incident: Customer discovers their personal data on public website

severity_assessment.finding: Customer names, emails, phone numbers, purchase history
Sales and operations not affected, but reputation damaged
Unknown - attacker may still have access
Data cannot be unseen - must notify all customers

topics.topic_name: Business Continuity - RTO, RPO, Disaster Recovery Planning
topics.explanation: Business continuity is ensuring the business can keep operating after a disaster. Disaster recovery is the plan to restore systems and data.

business_continuity_overview.definition: Ability to maintain or quickly restore critical business functions after an incident
business_continuity_overview.purpose: Minimize business impact if disaster strikes
business_continuity_overview.includes: Planning, processes, backup systems, trained staff

rto_recovery_time_objective.what_it_is: Maximum acceptable time to restore a system or function after failure

examples.rto: 4 hours - Employees can be without email for few hours
30 minutes - Every minute of downtime costs money in lost sales
examples.rationale: Revenue directly depends on system availability

examples.rto: 24 hours - Employees use daily but have backup processes
examples.rationale: Important but can operate without it for a day

examples.rto: 5 minutes - Milliseconds of delay cost millions

how_to_calculate: Assess how long business can operate without this system
Consider financial impact per hour of downtime
Factor in customer impact and reputation
Set RTO based on business criticality

rpo_recovery_point_objective.what_it_is: Maximum acceptable data loss - how much data can you afford to lose?

examples.rpo: 1 hour - Backup every hour, can lose up to 1 hour of emails
5 minutes - Backup every 5 minutes, minimize financial loss
Real-time replication - Data synced continuously across multiple locations

examples.rationale: Documents change slowly, daily backup acceptable

rpo_recovery_point_objective.formula: More frequent backups = Lower RPO = Less data loss risk = Higher cost

rto_vs_rpo.rto: About time - How long until system is working again?
rto_vs_rpo.rpo: About data - How much data are we willing to lose?

example.rto_4_hours: Database must be running again by 6:00 PM
example.rpo_1_hour: Can restore from backup from 1:00 PM (lose 1 hour of data)
example.if_backup_at_noon: Restore to 12:00 noon, lose 2 hours of data (exceeds RPO)
example.implication: Backup frequency must be <= RPO to meet recovery objectives

what_it_includes: Document RTO and RPO for each system

recovery_strategies.description: Empty data center that can be activated in disaster
Data center with some systems ready, but not fully configured
Fully equipped data center running parallel to production
Continuous backup to cloud, can restore from cloud

critical_systems.strategy: Hot site in different region, real-time replication
Hourly backups to cloud, continuous replication

testing_and_maintenance.importance: Plans don't work if never tested
testing_types: Tabletop exercises - Team reviews plan and discusses actions
Simulation tests - Actually run some parts of recovery plan
Full-scale tests - Actually restore from backup and test full recovery
testing_and_maintenance.frequency: At least annually, more for critical systems
testing_and_maintenance.documentation: Keep plans updated, accessible to right people, regularly reviewed

topics.topic_name: Compliance Basics - ISO 27001, NIST, and Why Frameworks Matter
topics.explanation: Compliance frameworks are standards that organizations follow to demonstrate they have adequate security controls. They're not just bureaucracy - they improve security.

what_is_compliance.definition: Adhering to security standards, regulations, and best practices required by law or industry
what_is_compliance.difference_from_security: Security is protecting from attacks. Compliance is proving you're doing security properly.
why_it_matters: Legal requirements - Many industries legally require compliance
Customer trust - Shows you take security seriously
Business relationships - Partners may require compliance
Insurance - Cyber insurance often requires certain compliance levels
Incident response - Compliance frameworks help during incidents

iso_27001.what_it_is: International standard for information security management
iso_27001.scope: Applies to any organization wanting to manage information security
iso_27001.countries: Used globally, ISO = International Organization for Standardization
iso_27001.certification: Organization can be audited and certified as compliant
iso_27001.controls: 14 main categories including access control, cryptography, incident management, business continuity
iso_27001.cost: Expensive - requires documentation, implementation, and external audit

nist_cybersecurity_framework.what_it_is: Framework published by US National Institute of Standards and Technology
nist_cybersecurity_framework.scope: Primarily used in US, especially for critical infrastructure

five_functions.what_it_means: Understand your assets, risks, and threats
five_functions.examples: Asset inventory, risk assessment, threat modeling

five_functions.what_it_means: Implement safeguards to prevent or reduce impact of attacks
Act during and after security incident
Return to normal operations after incident

nist_cybersecurity_framework.benefit: Flexible, non-prescriptive framework adaptable to any organization

other_important_frameworks.framework: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
other_important_frameworks.requirement: Legal requirement if you process credit cards
other_important_frameworks.main_controls: Firewall, encryption, access control, vulnerability management, incident response

other_important_frameworks.framework: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)
other_important_frameworks.requirement: Legal requirement in US for health data handling
other_important_frameworks.main_controls: Administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for health data
other_important_frameworks.penalties: Fines up to millions of dollars for violations

other_important_frameworks.applies_to: Organizations processing data of EU citizens
other_important_frameworks.requirement: Legal requirement if you have EU customers
other_important_frameworks.main_controls: Data privacy, consent, breach notification, data subject rights
other_important_frameworks.penalties: Up to 4% of annual revenue for violations

other_important_frameworks.main_controls: Security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy
other_important_frameworks.types: Type 1 (one point in time), Type 2 (over 6+ months)

other_important_frameworks.applies_to: Any organization wanting practical security controls
other_important_frameworks.main_controls: 18 controls organized by priority (Basic, Foundational, Organizational)

compliance_implementation_process.action: Determine which standards apply to your organization based on industry, location, customers
Audit what you already have in place vs. what's required
Create roadmap to close gaps, prioritize by risk and effort
Deploy security controls, create policies, train staff
Maintain evidence of compliance - policies, procedures, training records, audit logs
If required, undergo third-party audit to verify compliance
Monitor compliance, update controls as threats evolve

compliance_vs_security_perspective.compliance_view: Follow the checklist - meet all requirements in framework
compliance_vs_security_perspective.security_view: Implement what makes sense for our risk profile
compliance_vs_security_perspective.balanced_approach: Frameworks provide guidance, but adapt to your specific situation
compliance_vs_security_perspective.risk: Following framework without understanding why = false sense of security
compliance_vs_security_perspective.example: Framework says encrypt all data. But what if low-sensitivity data? Still encrypt, but may be overkill.

topics.topic_name: Practical Activity - Threat Modeling, Risk Assessment, and Incident Response Planning
topics.explanation: Apply threat analysis and risk management concepts by performing threat modeling, calculating risks, and planning incident response.

activity_1.task_name: Task 1: Perform STRIDE Threat Modeling on a System
activity_1.objective: Identify security threats using STRIDE methodology
activity_1.system_description: Users create task lists, share with team members, set deadlines. Data stored in cloud database. Users access via web browser and mobile app.

flows: User enters task -> App -> API -> Database
User shares task -> App -> API -> Permissions table
User uploads file -> App -> Cloud storage

stride_analysis.threat: Spoofing - Attacker pretends to be legitimate user
stride_analysis.example: Attacker uses stolen authentication token to access someone else's tasks
stride_analysis.mitigation: Validate tokens on each request, implement MFA, use short expiration times

stride_analysis.example: Attacker changes priority or deadline of task to disrupt workflow
stride_analysis.mitigation: Use HTTPS to encrypt traffic, validate all input, use API authentication

stride_analysis.threat: Repudiation - User claims they didn't create a task
stride_analysis.example: User denies adding sensitive information to shared task
stride_analysis.mitigation: Log all actions with timestamps and user IDs, disable action deletion

stride_analysis.threat: Information Disclosure - Attacker views private tasks
stride_analysis.example: Attacker accesses another user's tasks by changing ID in URL
stride_analysis.mitigation: Verify user owns task before returning data, implement proper access control

stride_analysis.threat: Denial of Service - Attacker overloads API
stride_analysis.example: Attacker sends 1000 requests per second, API becomes unresponsive
stride_analysis.mitigation: Implement rate limiting, DDoS protection, load balancing

stride_analysis.threat: Elevation of Privilege - Regular user becomes admin
stride_analysis.example: User modifies role in browser storage to admin, can delete other users' tasks
stride_analysis.mitigation: Never trust client-side role, verify on server, implement proper authorization

step_by_step.high_priority: Threats with high likelihood and high impact
step_by_step.example: Information Disclosure of private tasks is high priority

activity_1.output: Threat list with identified threats and proposed mitigations

threats_to_analyze.mitigation: Mandatory security training, phishing simulation, email filtering

risk_ranking: 2. Unencrypted hard drive - Risk 0.38 (38%) - FIX SECOND

classification_questions: Is access ongoing or past event? (ONGOING - very bad)
How much data was accessed? (Email history, potentially all sent/received emails)

scenarios.timeline: Fix within 2 weeks during normal patching

classification_questions: Are attempts succeeding? (No - being blocked by WAF)
Can attacks be prevented? (Yes - WAF already blocking)

units.title: Unit 8: Penetration Testing and Ethical Hacking
units.description: Understand how to legally test security by attempting to break in

modules.title: Penetration Testing and Ethical Hacking
modules.description: Understand how to legally test security by attempting to break in

critical_warning.headline: LEGAL AUTHORIZATION IS MANDATORY
critical_warning.message: Only perform penetration testing on systems you own or have explicit written permission to test. Unauthorized access is illegal.
violations: Accessing systems without permission is a felony in most countries

topics.topic_name: Penetration Testing Methodology - NIST, OWASP, PTES Frameworks
topics.explanation: Penetration testing follows structured methodologies to ensure comprehensive security testing. Different frameworks provide different approaches but share common phases.

what_is_penetration_testing.definition: Authorized attempt to compromise security of a system to identify vulnerabilities
what_is_penetration_testing.vs_vulnerability_assessment: Vulnerability assessment finds weaknesses. Penetration testing exploits them to assess real-world impact.
what_is_penetration_testing.legal_requirement: Must have written authorization from system owner. Period. No exceptions.
types: Black box - Attacker has zero knowledge of system
White box - Attacker has full knowledge (source code, architecture)
Gray box - Attacker has partial knowledge (like employee with some access)

nist_sp_800_115.what_it_is: US National Institute of Standards and Technology technical security testing framework
nist_sp_800_115.scope: Comprehensive technical testing including network, web, wireless, physical

owasp_testing_guide.what_it_is: Framework specifically for testing web applications

ptes_penetration_testing_execution_stand.what_it_is: Framework developed by security professionals for practical penetration testing
ptes_penetration_testing_execution_stand.focus: Comprehensive testing from reconnaissance to reporting

framework_comparison.aspect: NIST is very comprehensive and methodical
framework_comparison.owasp: OWASP is specific to web applications
framework_comparison.reality: Most real-world tests use combination of all three

topics.topic_name: Reconnaissance - Passive and Active Information Gathering
topics.explanation: Reconnaissance is gathering information about target before attempting to exploit. Passive gathering doesn't interact with target. Active gathering does.

reconnaissance_importance.why_it_matters: Good reconnaissance leads to successful penetration testing
reconnaissance_importance.percentage: Reconnaissance is often 30-50% of penetration test effort
reconnaissance_importance.goal: Understand target as deeply as possible before attempting exploitation

passive_reconnaissance.what_it_is: Gathering information WITHOUT directly interacting with target
passive_reconnaissance.benefit: Target doesn't know they're being tested
passive_reconnaissance.legal_status: Generally legal - public information is available to anyone

techniques.what_to_do: Google for company name, domain, employees, technology
techniques.finds: Exposed admin pages, confidential documents, employee emails

techniques.example: LinkedIn shows employees, their roles, skills. GitHub shows code and developers.

techniques.information: WHOIS records show domain owner, admin contact, creation date
techniques.finds: Company address, admin email, when domain was registered

what_they_reveal: Technologies they use (job requires experience with X framework)
New initiatives (hiring for DevOps suggests infrastructure changes)
techniques.example: Job posting for AWS security engineer suggests they use AWS

techniques.finds: Business strategy, technology decisions, security practices

techniques.tool: Wayback Machine - archives web pages from past
techniques.finds: Old website versions, leaked information that was later removed

active_reconnaissance.what_it_is: Gathering information BY directly interacting with target
active_reconnaissance.legal_requirement: Must be authorized - active reconnaissance on unauthorized target is illegal

techniques.what_it_does: Sends packets to find active hosts and open ports
techniques.finds: All active servers, open ports, services running

techniques.goal: Find all subdomains of target domain
techniques.finds: API servers, dev servers, internal tools, redundant systems

techniques.method: Call company pretending to be vendor or employee
techniques.legal_note: Must be authorized and disclosed in testing scope
Must be authorized, stay on public property

contents: List of all discovered hosts and IP addresses

topics.topic_name: Scanning and Enumeration - Finding Targets and Services
topics.explanation: Scanning identifies active hosts and open ports. Enumeration identifies services and versions. Together they map the target landscape.

scanning_vs_enumeration.scanning: Are there hosts? Which ports are open?
scanning_vs_enumeration.enumeration: What services? What versions? What information can I gather?

port_scanning.what_it_is: Sending packets to ports to determine if they're open

common_ports.risk: Can be exploited for email spoofing

scan_types.what_it_does: Complete TCP connection to each port
Send SYN, receive SYN-ACK, send RST (don't complete connection)
scan_types.detection: Harder to detect than connect scan

scan_types.what_it_does: Send UDP packets to identify open UDP ports
scan_types.accuracy: Less accurate (no response = open or filtered)
scan_types.speed: Very slow (UDP is slower than TCP)

scan_types.what_it_does: Send ACK packets to determine if port is filtered
scan_types.purpose: Map firewall rules, not find open ports

common_commands.what_it_does: Basic scan of target, shows open ports

nmap_tool.output_example: 21/tcp open ftp vsftpd 3.0.3, 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 7.4

techniques.what_it_does: Connect to service and read welcome message
techniques.example: telnet target.com 21 shows FTP server type and version
SSH server announces OpenSSH 7.4, which has known vulnerabilities

techniques.what_it_does: Try default username and password combinations

vulnerability_detection.automated_scanning: Vulnerability scanners automatically identify known vulnerabilities
what_they_find: Outdated software versions with known CVEs

topics.topic_name: Exploitation - Common Techniques and Tools
topics.explanation: Exploitation is using vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access or capabilities. This is the core of penetration testing.
topics.critical_legal_note: Only exploit systems you have written authorization to test. Unauthorized exploitation is a federal crime.

exploitation_process.step3: Prepare exploit (write code or download existing exploit)

common_exploitation_targets.example: Try all passwords against SSH until one works

common_exploitation_targets.exploitation: Insert SQL code into input fields
common_exploitation_targets.example: Username: ' OR '1'='1' -- logs in without password

common_exploitation_targets.vulnerability: Ability to execute arbitrary code on server
common_exploitation_targets.exploitation: Send malicious code to be executed
common_exploitation_targets.example: Vulnerable web app executes code from query parameter

common_exploitation_targets.exploitation: Exploit kernel bug or misconfig to gain root
common_exploitation_targets.example: Regular user runs command that executes as root

common_exploitation_targets.exploitation: Upload web shell that executes commands
common_exploitation_targets.example: Upload .php file that executes system commands

exploitation_frameworks.what_it_is: Comprehensive framework with thousands of exploits

exploit_databases.use: Research existing exploits for known CVEs

exploit_databases.note: Be very careful - many POCs are for educational research only
Restricted access, only for authorized security researchers

payload_concepts.what_is_payload: Code that executes after successful exploitation

common_payloads.what_it_does: Attacker gains command-line access to compromised system
Advanced payload with many post-exploitation features
Opens port on target, attacker connects to it
Uploads file to web server, provides web-based shell

exploitation_example.vulnerability: Remote Code Execution in Apache Struts 2
attack_flow: Struts parses expression and executes it
Attacker has command-line access to server
exploitation_example.tools: Custom exploit code or Metasploit module

topics.topic_name: Post-Exploitation - Maintaining Access, Data Exfiltration, Covering Tracks
topics.explanation: After initial compromise, attackers need to maintain access, find valuable data, and hide evidence of the breach. Penetration testers demonstrate this to show true impact.
post_exploitation_objectives: Pivot to other systems on network

privilege_escalation.what_it_is: Getting from low-privilege user to administrator/root
privilege_escalation.why_it_matters: Initial access often gets limited-privilege account. Need admin for full control.

techniques.example: Linux kernel bug allows user to become root
User can run any command as root without password
techniques.check: sudo -l shows what user can run as root

techniques.example: Sensitive file readable by all users
techniques.find: Configuration files or scripts owned by root but readable by all

techniques.what_they_are: Programs that run with owner's privileges
techniques.vulnerability: Vulnerable SUID binary can be exploited to become owner (usually root)

techniques.find: Plaintext passwords in scripts, config files, or memory

persistence_mechanisms.what_they_are: Methods to maintain access even if initial compromise is detected
persistence_mechanisms.importance: Initial foothold could be lost. Persistence ensures long-term access.

techniques.what_it_does: Create new admin account attacker controls
Add attacker's public key to authorized_keys
Upload executable file to web server
techniques.example: PHP file that executes system commands via web interface

techniques.benefit: Makes it harder to detect compromise
techniques.downside: Complex to install, may be detected by security software

techniques.what_it_does: Inject malicious code into running process

data_exfiltration.what_it_is: Stealing sensitive data from compromised system

methods.how: Copy files to attacker's server using scp, sftp, or http
methods.risk: Network traffic is visible to IDS

methods.why: Smaller files transfer faster, less likely to be detected
Even if traffic is captured, data is unreadable

methods.how: Move data to web-accessible directory, download via HTTP
methods.why: Mixes with legitimate traffic, may bypass DLP

methods.how: Transfer small amounts over long period

methods.why: DNS is rarely monitored, very stealthy

covering_tracks.why_pentesters_don't: Should leave evidence so organization knows what happened

techniques_to_demonstrate.problem: Delete all logs before login appears suspicious

techniques_to_demonstrate.example: Edit logs to remove traces of attacker activity
techniques_to_demonstrate.issue: Requires knowing log format, easy to miss something

techniques_to_demonstrate.goal: Make it appear file hasn't been modified

covering_tracks.why_it_fails: Modern systems have multiple logging mechanisms, backup logs in different locations, immutable audit trails

post_exploitation_tools.what_it_allows: After successful exploit, maintain interactive session with target

post_exploitation_tools.function: Extract passwords and credentials from Windows memory

post_exploitation_tools.focus: Post-exploitation on Windows systems using PowerShell

post_exploitation_tools.function: Map Active Directory relationships to find privilege escalation paths

topics.topic_name: Reporting - Presenting Findings to Stakeholders
topics.explanation: The final step is communicating findings to the organization in a clear, actionable way. A great report can drive security improvements.
why_reporting_matters: Organization needs to understand what was found
Executives need business impact, not technical jargon
Technical staff need detailed remediation guidance
Report should drive funding and priority for fixes

content: Overall risk rating (Critical, High, Medium, Low)
Number of vulnerabilities found by severity
penetration_test_report_structure.avoid: Technical jargon and detailed exploit information

penetration_test_report_structure.audience: Technical staff who will fix issues

content: Trend analysis (improved or worsened since last test)

for_each: Quick wins (easy fixes with big impact)
penetration_test_report_structure.example: Enable HTTPS (quick win), implement WAF (medium), redesign authentication (long-term)

contains: Technical details not needed by executives

critical_vulnerability_example.name: SQL Injection in Login Form
critical_vulnerability_example.description: The login form at https://target.com/login is vulnerable to SQL injection. User input is not properly validated or parameterized.
critical_vulnerability_example.proof_of_concept: Username: ' OR '1'='1' -- Password: anything Results in successful login without valid credentials.
critical_vulnerability_example.impact: Complete database compromise. Attacker can read all customer data, modify records, or delete everything.
critical_vulnerability_example.remediation: Use parameterized queries. Example: query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=? AND password=?' with parameters bound separately.

metrics_in_report.metric: Percentage of systems with critical findings
metrics_in_report.example: 30% of systems have at least one critical vulnerability

communication_tips.action: Executives get business impact, technical staff get how-to fix
Not 'weak password policy' but 'system allows 4-character passwords'
Screenshots, proof-of-concept code, actual system outputs
Not 'data could be stolen' but 'up to 50,000 customer records exposed'
Not 'improve security' but 'enable HTTPS on port 443'
Goal is to help, not embarrass. Professional, constructive tone.

topics.topic_name: Legal and Ethical Boundaries - Authorization, Scope, Laws
topics.explanation: Penetration testing must be legal and ethical. Crossing the line from authorized testing to hacking is a serious crime.

critical_legal_warning.headline: THIS IS NOT OPTIONAL
points: Unauthorized computer access is a federal crime in most countries
Permanent criminal record destroys career prospects

legal_requirements.what_it_means: Must have explicit written permission from system owner
must_include: Date and time range for testing
Escalation procedures if something goes wrong
Signature from authorized person with authority
legal_requirements.red_flags: No written contract = do not proceed, no matter what verbal agreement says

what_it_includes: Specific IP addresses and domains authorized
What's off-limits (e.g., 'do not test payment processing')
legal_requirements.importance: Prevents accidental testing of systems you shouldn't touch

legal_requirements.means: Testing must be done by qualified professionals
legal_requirements.credentials: Security certifications (OSCP, CEH, GPEN) or extensive experience
legal_requirements.accountability: Testers must be held accountable for their actions

in_scope: Specific IP ranges or domains listed in contract
out_of_scope: Any systems NOT listed in contract
Systems of other companies or third parties
Customer data systems (unless explicitly in scope)
Test outside authorized methods (e.g., only vulnerability scan, not exploitation)

legal_considerations.law: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) - United States
legal_considerations.penalty: Up to 10 years in prison, fines up to $250,000+
legal_considerations.exception: Only legal if authorized by system owner

legal_considerations.what_it_prohibits: Unauthorized access, modification, or disruption of computer systems

legal_considerations.law: Data Protection Regulations - EU (GDPR) and others
legal_considerations.penalty: Fines up to 4% of revenue for GDPR

legal_considerations.requirement: If you access customer data, may need to notify affected individuals

ethical_boundaries.means: Don't cause system outages or damage
ethical_boundaries.example: Don't delete data, don't disrupt operations, don't DoS the server
ethical_boundaries.rule: If you break something, report and fix it

ethical_boundaries.means: Take only data necessary to demonstrate vulnerability
ethical_boundaries.example: If you can read customer data, read a few records to prove it, not all million records
ethical_boundaries.responsibility: Only access what's needed for testing

ethical_boundaries.what_it_means: Report findings confidentially before public disclosure
ethical_boundaries.timeline: Typically 90 days to fix before going public
ethical_boundaries.purpose: Give organization time to patch before exploit goes viral

ethical_boundaries.don't_do: Don't post exploits online, don't tell employees, don't brag about findings

don't_do: Don't use findings for personal gain

scenario_1.title: Proper Authorization
scenario_1.situation: Your company asks you to test internal web application
steps: 1. Get written authorization from CTO with specific scope
2. Authorization includes: IP address, date/time window, methods allowed
outcome : LEGAL - Successful security improvement for company

scenario_2.title: NO Authorization
scenario_2.situation: Your friend says 'you can test my cousin's company website to help'
problem: Your friend is not authorized to give permission
scenario_2.correct_action: Decline. Ask for written authorization from company owner.

key_lessons: ALWAYS get written authorization before testing any system
Verbal permission is not sufficient legal protection
Scope must be specific - no guessing about what's allowed
If in doubt, don't test. Unauthorized access is a crime.
Professional reputation depends on ethical conduct
